body:
OpenGP5 is free, open source firmware for the Valeton GP-5 guitar pedal. It runs the pedal’s sound, screen and controls. You can use an effect we provide or write your own in C.
OpenGP5 contains no code or data from Valeton or the chip vendor. To go back to Valeton’s firmware, follow Recovery. That guide also covers the DSP update fault that can block a USB flash.
Where to start I want to… Read Try an effect on my pedal Get started Load captures, edit presets or back up my data Launchpad Learn an effect’s controls Firmware Write my own effect Build a firmware, then Your first effect Look up a function or protocol API reference, Protocols Fix a problem Recovery, Help What each part does Firmware runs on the pedal. NAM Loader plays Neural Amp Modeler (NAM) captures: models of how an amp or pedal sounds. Dreamcatcher loops and processes your playing. The tremolo makes the volume rise and fall. Only one firmware build runs on the pedal at a time.
Launchpad is the desktop app. Use it to flash firmware, load captures and edit presets as you play. It also loads cabinet impulse responses (cab IRs): files that add a speaker cabinet’s sound. Its backups save the data each supported firmware exposes. With Valeton’s firmware, a backup holds the 100 presets; export SnapTones and user IRs in Valeton Suite.
The web flasher installs firmware from Chrome, Edge or Opera on a computer. You do not need to install an app.
The platform is the shared code for firmware authors. It handles both chips, USB, the screen, controls and storage. Your code defines the sound and interface.
Note These docs target platform 1.0.0. Its API, the set of functions and commands firmware can use, doesn’t change in a way that breaks a firmware for all of 1.x. See Beta testing to report how your pedal works.

body:
Warning A flash can fail. Valeton does not make or endorse this project.
What can go wrong A failed flash may need another flash. The factory loader starts the pedal’s USB update mode. The USB update tools cannot overwrite this loader. If a flash stops or the firmware fails to start, use the controls to enter update mode and try again. Recovery gives the steps.
Some pedals have a DSP update fault. The fault can block OpenGP5 and Valeton updates. These pedals may need an FT232H USB debug board wired to pads inside the case. You must open the pedal and may need to solder the wires. See J7 recovery.
As of November 2026, reports describe this fault on four of about seven pedals that tried OpenGP5. This small sample does not show how often the fault occurs across all GP-5s. It is a fault in the pedal’s DSP updater, not evidence that an OpenGP5 flash caused it. Read Known limits before you decide to flash.
Back up first Switching to a different firmware erases the old firmware’s data. Back up before you start the flash. Launchpad may clear the data before it writes the new firmware, so a failed flash can still leave the data erased.
On OpenGP5: use Launchpad’s Backups page to save the installed build’s presets, settings and files. The app also offers a backup when you switch, if it can read the pedal. On Valeton’s firmware: Launchpad can save the 100 presets. Export SnapTones and user IRs in Valeton Suite; Launchpad cannot back them up. Global settings stay on the pedal. An update with the same firmware ID keeps its storage. Check the release notes for any changes to saved settings. A renamed setting, for example, may return to its default.
During a flash Use a USB cable you trust. Plug it into the computer. Keep the pedal plugged in and powered until the tool says it has restarted. A flash takes about 40 seconds. Keep the app or browser tab open while it writes. Launchpad asks before it closes during a flash. To help test a pedal, see Beta testing.

Plug the pedal into your computer and open Flash. You can also start with the pedal in update mode. Under Choose a firmware, choose one of the sources below. Read the notice about stored data. Other authors’ builds carry the label Not reviewed. The file checks do not include a review of the code.

body:
NAM Loader plays Neural Amp Modeler (NAM) captures on the GP-5. A capture models the sound of an amp or pedal. NAM Loader runs at 48 kHz and supports A2 captures. It uses their A2-Lite model; older A1 captures do not work.
Version 1.3 or later holds 30 captures and 12 cabinet impulse responses (cab IRs). An IR adds a speaker cabinet’s sound. Each capture keeps its own IR choice, noise gate and 3-band EQ. You can choose any stored IR, or none.
Source and releases on GitHub
Controls The screen has two main pages. NAM shows the playing capture; CAB shows its IR. Two dots in the header mark the current page.
Control Action Turn PARA Switch NAM / CAB pages; in a list, move the highlight Press PARA Open the capture list on NAM or the IR list on CAB; press again to load the highlighted item Hold PARA for 0.6 s Open or close TONE to edit the playing capture’s gate and EQ Press the foot switch Toggle bypass Turn the volume knob Set the output level The playing capture keeps sounding while you browse. The list closes after five seconds with no knob movement. The screen shows the capture or IR name, slot number, input level and output volume. Long names scroll. The pedal recalls the last capture at power-on.
Set the gate and EQ Hold PARA for 0.6 seconds to open TONE. Turn PARA to select GATE, BASS, MID or TREBLE. Press PARA, then turn it to change the value. Press again to select another row. Hold PARA to leave TONE, or wait ten seconds without using the control. The pedal saves changes about two seconds after the last edit. Keep it powered until then.
Getting captures onto the pedal Use Launchpad’s Tones page. Drop a .nam file, check its name and click Send to slot. Launchpad converts the model and sends it to the pedal. Use the same page to send .wav cab IRs. With no stored captures, NAM Loader plays its built-in demo.
Cab IRs Use an IR with an amp-only, or DI, capture. A full-rig capture includes the cab sound, so choose NONE for that capture.
Launchpad converts each IR to 48 kHz and keeps up to 1,024 samples (21 ms). It also adjusts the level. A capture uses the IR with the same slot number by default, if that IR exists. You can choose another or NONE. If the processor runs out of time, NAM Loader turns off the IR to keep the audio running. How the model runs NAM Loader keeps the A2-Lite model’s layers. It converts weights to 16-bit fixed-point values and uses a 32-bit signal through the network. Rounding changes the precision of the weights; it does not retrain the model.
Fixed-point maths lets the model fit the pedal’s time budget. Its output differs from NAM’s floating-point output. The size of that difference depends on the capture and input signal.
Both chips share the work. The digital signal processor (DSP) runs the first layers. The control chip runs the rest, plus the output stage and cab IR.
Input level and loudness Launchpad offers two gain controls when it converts a capture. Both start on:
Calibrate sets input gain to match the level used to make the capture. The file must include that level. The pedal reaches full scale at an input of +7.1 dBu. Normalize sets output gain with a test sound. It aims for a level of −20 dB below full scale. It uses K-weighting to account for the ear’s response to low and high sounds. It also keeps peaks in that test no higher than −3 dBFS. The peak limit can keep a capture below the loudness target. Your playing can also produce different levels from the test signal. With Normalize off, Launchpad keeps the capture’s output gain. These two switches change gain, not the model’s layers or training.
Updating An update keeps your captures, IRs and settings. Files sent before version 1.1 did not use Calibrate or Normalize. To use those options, send the source .nam file again. Then check its gate, EQ and IR choice.
Versions Version Changes 1.3.1 Launchpad can select the playing capture with Play on the pedal 1.3.0 30 captures, a separate bank of 12 IRs, and NAM / CAB pages 1.2.0 Noise gate and 3-band EQ per capture 1.1.0 Cab IRs, 48 kHz, Calibrate and Normalize 1.0.0 First release with 12 capture slots

body:
Install the tools, build the tremolo, and try it on your computer. You need a pedal to flash and play the build. Download time depends on your connection.
What you need Git, Python 3.9 or later, and a C compiler (cc) for tests on your computer. A Valeton GP-5 and USB cable for flashing. The tools for your system below. System Tools macOS Xcode command line tools (xcode-select --install) and Docker Desktop; start Docker before building Linux (x86_64) curl and a 32-bit C runtime; see the commands below Windows Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) with Ubuntu for builds; Windows Python for USB flashing The tool that builds code for the control chip runs on Linux. On macOS, Docker runs that tool. On Linux, add the 32-bit C runtime for your system:
Linux system Command Debian, Ubuntu sudo apt install libc6-i386 Arch sudo pacman -S lib32-glibc Fedora sudo dnf install glibc.i686 For flashing, add these MIDI tools to the Python setup that can see the pedal:
pip install mido python-rtmidi For screen images in the simulator, install Pillow with pip install pillow. For the DSP emulator, install Unicorn with pip install unicorn. These tools are optional if you do not use those checks.
Get OpenGP5 and the compilers Run the build commands in Terminal on macOS, a Linux shell, or an Ubuntu WSL shell on Windows:
git clone https://github.com/OpenGP5/OpenGP5.git cd OpenGP5 release/setup-toolchain.sh The setup script gets both build tools from Andes and Arm, about 190 MB in total. It checks each file’s checksum and keeps the tools in fw-build/. It makes no system-wide changes. Each computer uses the same pinned tool versions.
Build From the OpenGP5 folder, run:
platform/build_firmware.sh tremolo The build combines the tremolo’s sound and control code in build/GP-5_tremolo.bin. This image holds the DSP firmware and the control chip’s app. The DSP is the digital signal processor that handles sound.
Try it on the computer python3 tools/simulate.py tremolo The simulator runs the sound, screen and scripted controls. It saves the results as files and has no live window. See The simulator for input audio and control scripts.
Flash Read Before you flash and back up your data. Plug the pedal into the computer. On macOS or Linux, run these commands from the OpenGP5 folder:
python3 tools/gp5tool.py status python3 tools/gp5tool.py flash build/GP-5_tremolo.bin --sections all On Windows, flash with Windows Python. WSL cannot see the pedal’s USB-MIDI ports. Copy the built .bin to a Windows copy of the OpenGP5 folder, beside tools. Open PowerShell in that folder:
py -3 tools/gp5tool.py status py -3 tools/gp5tool.py flash GP-5_tremolo.bin --sections all You can also choose the built file in Launchpad or the web flasher. status checks that the tool can find the pedal. A flash takes about 40 seconds. If the pedal does not return, see Recovery.
Next Read How a firmware works, then build Your first effect. To keep the code in your own project, use Your own repository.

body:
Use this checklist to test your GP-5 and report the results. Allow about an hour. Reports of passed checks and faults both help. Send yours with the hardware report form.
Before you start: OpenGP5 is alpha software. Some pedals have a DSP updater fault that blocks USB updates, including Valeton’s updates. Those pedals may need a USB debug board wired inside the case. Read Known limits and the backup steps before you take part.
You need A GP-5, USB cable and desktop or laptop computer. Launchpad, or Chrome / Edge for the web flasher. A backup of the data you want to keep. With Valeton’s firmware, save the 100 presets in Launchpad. Export SnapTones and user IRs in Valeton Suite; Launchpad cannot back them up. Write down the name and version of the installed build. Note any version printed on the board or case. If Launchpad offers Back up first, choose it. The app does not make that choice for you.
The checklist Tick each check that passes. For a failure, write down the steps and what you saw.
1. Flashing
Launchpad or the web flasher finds the pedal. Flash the tremolo. The flash completes and the pedal restarts into it. If the DSP section stalls at its start, stop testing and report the error. If no DSP data was written, unplugging and reconnecting lets the old build run. See J7 recovery for the known updater fault. 2. The tremolo
The guitar comes through and the volume knob sets output level. Turn PARA: the highlight moves through RATE, DEPTH, SHAPE and PRESET. Press PARA and turn it: the value changes and you hear it. Press again to finish editing. Sine, Triangle and Square shapes sound smooth, without clicks. The foot switch turns the effect off (dim red LEDs, grey values) and on (mint LEDs). On PRESET, hold PARA for 0.6 seconds. The screen confirms the saved slot, such as Saved P1. After a save completes, unplug and reconnect. The saved settings and preset return. 3. Updating and switching firmware
Flash the tremolo again. Its settings stay. Flash Dreamcatcher. It starts with its own defaults. The looper, delay and reverb respond to the controls. Open Launchpad’s Presets page. Changes in the live editor change the sound. Use Save to store the current sound, then reload it to check the result. 4. Recovery (optional)
Unplug the pedal. Press and hold the foot switch and PARA as you reconnect it, then release both. Launchpad or the web flasher reports update mode. Flash a working build from update mode. 5. Going back
Flash Valeton’s firmware from Launchpad. The pedal starts with factory presets. Restore the Valeton preset backup from Launchpad’s Backups page. Your saved presets return. Import exported SnapTones and user IRs in Valeton Suite, if you had any. Reporting Open a hardware report and include:
this checklist with passed and failed checks; your original Valeton firmware version; the tested effect, platform and Launchpad versions; your computer’s operating system; error text and logs; if you have Python, output from python3 tools/gp5tool.py status and python3 tools/gp5_link.py stats. Ask questions in Discussions.

body:
Dreamcatcher records as you play. Tap the foot switch to loop a short part of your playing. Add delay, pitch shifts or reverb to the loop or your live sound.
The dry signal is your guitar without effects. The wet signal has effects. The delay can break sound into grains, which are short slices that can shift pitch, reverse or repeat. A slow control wave, the LFO (low-frequency oscillator), sets the pace of modulation and chance events.
Chase Bliss MOOD MKII and Old Blood Noise Endeavors Parting inspired the effect. Dreamcatcher has no affiliation with either company and contains none of their code.
Source and releases on GitHub
Controls Control Action Turn PARA Select a setting; the screen shows its section and value Turn the volume knob Edit the selected setting after a small move; gold text shows that the knob has taken control Tap the foot switch Catch a loop, or release it and record new playing Hold the foot switch Add sound to a playing loop (DUB); while listening, freeze the wet signal (FRZ) Press PARA Save the sound to the active preset, except when choosing a different preset; see below Hold PARA for 3 s Toggle the effect; bypass keeps the dry signal unchanged and retains the caught loop Overdub (DUB) adds your playing to the loop until you release the foot switch. Freeze (FRZ) holds the wet sound while you hold the switch.
When you select a setting, it keeps its value until you move the volume knob a small amount. The knob then sets the value from its own position, which can cause a jump. It edits the selected setting; select VOLUME to set output level.
The LEDs glow violet when the effect is on and dim red when it is off. The header dot pulses at the LFO rate.
A good start Play a chord and tap the foot switch to catch it as a loop. Set ROUTE to IN+LOOP so the effects process both your guitar and the loop. Raise SMEAR and set CHANCE a little above its middle value. Lower CLOCK, then play over the loop. In the tables, noon means the middle of a setting’s range. The knob must take control before its position sets the value.
Settings Tempo sync needs Dreamcatcher 1.4 or later. Other tables describe the controls shared by these builds.
MAIN Setting What it does PRESET Select one of 8 saved sounds; press PARA to load the highlighted slot MIX Blend dry and wet; the middle gives both at full level CLOCK Set the engine’s sample rate, from 1.4 to 44 kHz in musical steps SYNC Choose FREE timing or SYNC to the BPM tempo BPM Set tempo from 40 to 240 beats per minute VOLUME Set output level On PRESET, pressing PARA loads a highlighted saved slot or saves into an empty one. With the active slot highlighted, it saves the current sound. Away from PRESET, pressing PARA also saves to the active slot. A preset holds all settings, including VOLUME.
P3 means preset 3 is active. P3* means its sound has changed since the last save. 3 EMPTY marks an empty slot. SAVED P3 confirms a save.
A lower CLOCK gives longer loops and delays, with a rougher sound. Changing CLOCK during a loop shifts its pitch in musical steps. In SYNC mode, TIME, RATE, LENGTH and GRAIN use note lengths, and the LFO follows the beat. A dot means a dotted note, T means a triplet, and BAR means one bar.
WET Setting What it does TIME Set delay time: 4 ms to 1.16 s at 44 kHz, or up to 37 s at lower CLOCK values SMEAR Blend distinct echoes into dense reverb through diffusion and feedback TONE Darken each repeat; OPEN removes that darkening CHANCE Set how often sound enters or feeds back through the delay GLITCH Set delay-clock speed or let the LFO choose it at random With SYNC, TIME spans 1/32 note to 1 bar.
CHANCE has three regions:
Below noon, it sets the chance that input enters the delay on each LFO cycle. At noon, the delay takes all input (ALWAYS). Above noon, input keeps entering and feedback becomes more likely (FB). GLITCH also changes behavior across its range:
Below noon, choose HALF, NORMAL or DOUBLE delay-clock speed. Above noon, each LFO cycle has a growing chance to choose a new clock speed and crush amount (RND). GRAIN Setting What it does GRAIN Set slice length: 6 to 186 ms at 44 kHz; with SYNC, 1/64 to 1/16 note PITCH Set the chance that a grain shifts to an interval in SCALE SCALE Choose OCT UP, OCT DN, OCTAVES, 5TH+OCT or HARMONY REVERSE Set the chance that a grain plays in reverse STUTTER Set the chance that a grain repeats the one before it Feeding pitch-shifted repeats back into the delay builds a shimmer.
MOD Setting What it does RATE Set LFO speed: 0.05 to 12 Hz; with SYNC, 1/32 note to 4 bars per cycle DEPTH Set the amount of modulation SHAPE Choose SINE, SQUARE, RAMP, SAW, RND SIN, RND SQR or ENV MOD Apply TREMOLO (volume changes) or VIBRATO (pitch changes) to the wet signal RATE also sets how often CHANCE makes a choice. With ENV, your playing level opens the delay and CHANCE becomes SENSE, the sensitivity control.
COLOR Setting What it does DISSOLVE Below noon, reduce sample rate (LOFI); at noon, CLEAN; above noon, reverse at full, ½, ¼ or ⅛ speed FILTER Below noon, low-pass from 150 Hz to 13 kHz; at noon, OPEN; above noon, high-pass from 20 Hz to 2.5 kHz A low-pass filter cuts highs. A high-pass filter cuts lows.
LOOP Setting What it does MODE Choose TAPE or STRETCH LENGTH Set loop length in TAPE mode or slice length in STRETCH mode SPEED / DRIFT Set tape speed and direction, or how fast the slices move LOOP LV Set the loop’s level and how much it feeds the effects FADE Set how much old sound remains on each overdub pass: REPLACE to 100 % ROUTE Process IN (guitar), IN+LOOP or LOOP in the wet channel In TAPE mode, LENGTH spans 1/16 of memory to all of it: up to 1.47 seconds at 44 kHz or 47 seconds at 1.4 kHz. With SYNC, it spans 1/8 note to 4 bars. SPEED spans REV 4X to 4X.
In STRETCH mode, LENGTH sets slice size. DRIFT moves through slices in reverse or forward, with FROZEN at noon to hold the position.
REVERB Setting What it does DECAY Set tail length from 0.3 to 27 s; HOLD sustains the tail and blocks new input MIX Blend from no reverb, through effect plus reverb at the middle, to reverb alone SIZE Change room size from a room to a large hall PRE-DLY Wait 0 to 200 ms before reverb starts MOD Add slow pitch drift to the tail SHIMMER Feed an octave-up copy of the tail back into the reverb Reverb MIX changes the wet path. Your dry guitar stays dry.
Presets in Launchpad Use Launchpad’s Presets page to edit sounds as you play and save them. You can name, import, export and move the 8 preset slots. Use Write to pedal to save slot edits. Backups save the set of presets to a file.

body:
Each tool checks the file before it writes to the pedal. It then starts update mode, writes the firmware, and waits for the pedal to restart. Read Before you flash and back up your data.
With Launchpad Use Launchpad if you also want to load captures, edit presets or make backups.
Install Launchpad and open it. Plug the pedal into the computer. Launchpad shows which firmware it runs. Open Flash and choose a build. Use Your own file for a .bin file. Read the data-loss notice. Tick the box that asks you to keep the pedal connected and accept the risk. Click the Flash button for the build you chose. If Launchpad offers Back up first, choose it to save your data. See the Flash page for the choices and data rules.
In your browser The web flasher needs no app installation.
Open it in Chrome, Edge or Opera on a computer. These browsers support Web MIDI, which the flasher uses. Plug the pedal in, click Connect, and allow MIDI access. Choose an available build, or upload a .bin file from a release or your own build. You can also upload Valeton’s firmware. Read the confirmation beside the checkbox, tick it, and click Flash. Safari lacks Web MIDI. Firefox asks for permission; use one of the browsers listed above for this guide.
From the command line Use the command-line tool for scripts or your own builds.
Download OpenGP5 from GitHub with Code › Download ZIP, or download a release’s source ZIP. Unzip it to get tools/gp5tool.py.
Install Python 3.9 or later, then install the MIDI libraries:
pip install mido python-rtmidi On Windows, flash with Windows Python. WSL, the Linux shell on Windows, cannot see the pedal’s USB-MIDI ports.
Download an image from a release, such as Dreamcatcher’s releases, or build one. Put the .bin in the unzipped OpenGP5 folder.
Plug the pedal in. Open a terminal in that folder, then run:
python3 tools/gp5tool.py status python3 tools/gp5tool.py flash GP-5_dreamcatcher.bin --sections all status checks whether the tool can find the pedal. Use your image’s filename in the flash command. On Windows, use py -3 in place of python3 if that is how you start Python.
Checking a download A checksum helps you check that a download matches the release file. Releases list checksums in SHA256SUMS. Run the command for your system and compare its result with the entry for your file:
System Command macOS, Linux shasum -a 256 GP-5_dreamcatcher.bin Windows certutil -hashfile GP-5_dreamcatcher.bin SHA256 What gets written An OpenGP5 image holds code for two chips. The digital signal processor (DSP) handles sound. The control chip runs the screen, controls and USB.
The flash tool keeps the factory loader in place. A full Valeton image also holds its models and presets.

body:
This guide explains the two chips, the shared code, and how your effect uses them. Start here if you have not worked with the GP-5 hardware.
Two processors The GP-5 has two processors. A build has code for each one. The digital signal processor (DSP) handles audio. The control processor handles the screen, controls, USB and storage. It can also process audio through the audio link.
Part DSP Control processor Chip Arm Cortex-M4F, about 192 MHz Andes NDS32 (BP1048), 288 or 320 MHz Main task Mono guitar input, stereo output Screen, knobs, foot switch, LEDs, USB and storage Your code dsp/firmware.h nds32/*.c Calls fw_process() for each 64-sample block Control callbacks and fw_tick() every 10 ms Firmware RAM budget 19,712 bytes for variables; 122,880 for buffers 264,160 bytes for data; code runs from flash A block lasts 1.45 ms at 44.1 kHz or 1.33 ms at 48 kHz. The API version notes explain the memory guarantee for 1.x.
The platform The platform is the code both halves use for start-up, hardware access, USB, storage and the processor link. Your effect can use these tools without changing the platform. A callback is a function you write that the platform calls at a set time or on an event.
flowchart TB io(["Knobs, foot switch, screen, USB"]) <--> ctl ctl["`**Control processor** _The platform:_ drivers, USB, screen, storage, parameters, presets, log _Your code:_ fw_para_turn, fw_foot_down, fw_draw, on_block (optional)`"] ctl <== "the link: parameters, and audio (optional)" ==> dsp dsp["`**DSP** _Your code:_ fw_process, fw_param _The platform:_ audio in and out`"] dsp <--> audio(["Guitar in, out L / R"]) Callbacks must not wait for events or contain loops that block other work. Aim to finish a main-loop pass within one or two audio blocks. Draw the screen in strips so controls and USB can run between draws. fw_draw returns a non-zero value when it has more to draw. See Performance for the separate audio deadlines.
Settings: parameters Declare each setting as a parameter in params.h. The platform can then:
send a changed value to the DSP through fw_param(); keep values marked for saving across power-off; store values marked for presets in named slots; let a computer read and change them. Launchpad builds its Live editor from this list. See Parameters and presets.
Sound on both chips: the audio link The audio link exchanges 32-bit words after each audio block. Send guitar samples to the control chip, process them there, then read the result on the DSP. The result returns three blocks later: about 4.4 ms at 44.1 kHz or 4 ms at 48 kHz.
NAM Loader and Dreamcatcher share sound work this way. The control chip has more memory and can run some sound code faster. See The audio link.
USB audio and Bluetooth A firmware built for 1.0 is also a USB audio interface: the computer records its finished sound and can play through the pedal. It uses 64 words of the audio link each way, which the platform keeps for it. Set "usb_audio": false in firmware.json to turn it off and get them back. See USB audio.
With "bluetooth": true, the pedal also takes MIDI over Bluetooth: Launchpad and the phone remote can change settings and presets without a cable. See Bluetooth.
Storage The installed build owns about 300 KB of storage. Its id in firmware.json marks the storage as its own.
An update with the same ID keeps storage. Changes to parameter names can reset those settings. A different ID starts with empty storage. Returning to Valeton’s firmware restores its factory preset layout. Restore a backup to get your own presets back. The platform saves parameters marked with a save flag. Use store records for other small data, up to 1 KB per record. Use files for larger data that a computer writes, such as captures. See Storage.
What happens at power-on The control chip starts the platform and checks which build the storage belongs to. It loads saved parameters, then calls your fw_init(). It starts the DSP, which calls its own fw_init(). The DSP starts with defaults from params.h. The control chip then sends the saved values before audio fades in. The DSP calls fw_process() for each block. The control chip runs its main loop for callbacks, parameter changes, saving, USB and the screen. From code to pedal flowchart TB src["Your firmware: firmware.json, params.h, dsp/firmware.h, nds32/*.c"] src -- "platform/build_firmware.sh" --> bin["build/GP-5_<id>.bin: both parts, and a description of itself (name, version, author)"] bin -- "Launchpad, the web flasher, or gp5tool.py flash" --> pedal(["The pedal"]) Use tools/simulate.py to check the sound, screen and controls on your computer before flashing. See The simulator. For a pedal that fails to start, follow Recovery, including the known DSP update fault.
Next, build Your first effect, or start a separate repository with the firmware template.

Use it to load Neural Amp Modeler (NAM) captures: models of how an amp or pedal sounds. It also loads cabinet impulse responses (cab IRs) for the sound of a speaker cab.

xattr -cr "/Applications/OpenGP5 Launchpad.app" Windows: run the setup file. On Windows protected your PC, click More info, then Run anyway. If you chose a ZIP file, unzip it before you open the app.

body:
Use Tones with NAM Loader. Version 1.3 or later holds 30 captures and 12 cab IRs. A capture models an amp or pedal’s sound. A cabinet impulse response (cab IR) adds a speaker cabinet’s sound. Each capture can use any stored IR, or none.
The left column lists files on the pedal. Use NAM / IR to choose the list. The right column shows the selected file and controls for adding files.
Add a capture Choose NAM and select an empty slot. If you do not select one, Launchpad uses the first free slot. Drop a .nam file on the page, or click Choose file under Add a capture. Check Name on the pedal and click Send to slot, followed by the slot number. NAM Loader supports A2 captures, which include an A2-Lite model that fits the pedal. It runs that part of the capture. Older A1 files use a different model format and do not work.
Conversion Open Conversion to see two switches. Both start on:
Calibrate sets the input gain to match the level used to make the capture. It needs a capture file that includes this level. Normalize aims for a shared loudness target and limits peaks. Some captures may still sound louder than others. With this off, Launchpad keeps the capture’s output gain. Launchpad keeps the A2-Lite model’s layers and rounds its weights for fixed-point maths. That changes their precision. Calibrate and Normalize change gain; they do not retrain the model.
Add a cab IR Choose IR and select an empty slot. Drop a .wav file on the page, or click Choose file under Add an IR. Check the name and click Send to IR, followed by the slot number. Launchpad converts the sample rate to 48 kHz, keeps up to 1,024 samples (21 ms), and adjusts the level. Use a cab IR with an amp-only, or DI, capture. For a full-rig capture that includes the cab, choose NONE.
IRs added with NAM Loader 1.1 or 1.2 use an older format that takes twice the space. Shrink converts those IRs to the smaller format without changing their sound.
Edit a capture or IR Select a file in the list to see its controls:
Control Action Play on the pedal Switch to this capture; needs NAM Loader 1.3.1 or later Rename Change the name on the pedal Replace Load a new file into the same slot; read the reset rules below Remove Clear the slot IR Choose the capture’s cab IR, its default IR, or none Gate and EQ Set the noise gate, bass, mid and treble for this capture A new capture does not keep the old capture’s gate and EQ: it starts with the gate off and EQ flat. Check its IR choice after replacement. Replacing an IR changes the cabinet sound for every capture that uses that IR.
Gate and EQ affect the sound as you play. The pedal saves them with the capture. You can also edit a capture that is not playing; the next time you select it, the pedal uses those settings.
When the pedal is full To add a file when all its slots are full, replace or remove one. If old-format IRs use too much storage, Launchpad shrinks them to make room.
On the pedal Use Launchpad to load captures and cab IRs. On the pedal, choose which ones to play and set the gate and EQ. See NAM Loader’s controls.

It needs a firmware built with Bluetooth on ("bluetooth": true in its firmware.json, OpenGP5 1.0 or later), such as Dreamcatcher.

Open the phone remote, tap Connect and pick OpenGP5 (GP-5 on firmwares built before OpenGP5 1.0). The pedal doesn’t appear in the phone’s Bluetooth settings: phones list Bluetooth MIDI devices only inside the apps that use them. Connect from the page.
If the pedal doesn’t show up, something else is probably still connected to it: phones reconnect to a Bluetooth device in the background after an app has used it. Turn Bluetooth off on the other phone or computer.
Presets Load switches to a preset. Save writes the current sound into a slot on the pedal; the page asks first. Firmwares that keep preset names can be renamed from the pencil button.

Firmwares built on OpenGP5 1.0 make the pedal a USB audio interface, beside its MIDI port. There’s no driver to install. It works with any recording app on macOS and Windows. Linux should work too, since the device is class-compliant, but it hasn’t been tested yet.
It comes with Dreamcatcher 1.5, NAM Loader 1.4, the tremolo 1.2 and other firmwares built on 1.0, unless the firmware turns it off.
What the computer sees The pedal shows up as an audio device called OpenGP5, with 2 inputs and 2 outputs, 16-bit, at the firmware’s sample rate:
Firmware Sample rate Dreamcatcher, tremolo 44.1 kHz NAM Loader 48 kHz Set your recording app to the same rate. If the rate is different, the computer converts it, or the app refuses the device.
Record The inputs carry the firmware’s finished stereo sound: what you hear from the pedal, taken before the volume knob. Turning the knob changes what you hear, not what is recorded.
Play through the pedal The computer’s sound, a backing track or your DAW’s output, comes out of the pedal’s outputs, mixed with the pedal’s own sound. The volume knob sets the level of both.
Monitoring in a DAW If your DAW plays back the pedal’s input while it records (input monitoring), you hear the pedal twice: once straight from the pedal, and again a moment later from the DAW. To hear only the DAW:
In Launchpad, untick Pedal sound while the computer plays in the pedal panel, or run python3 tools/gp5_link.py direct off. This turns off only the pedal’s own sound at its outputs, and only while the computer is sending sound to the pedal. When the computer stops playing, you hear the pedal again. Recording doesn’t change. The setting goes back on when the pedal restarts.
If the device doesn’t show up or can’t be opened Check that the firmware is built on OpenGP5 1.0 or later. Launchpad’s pedal panel shows the platform. On Windows, if the device shows up but can’t be opened (Windows and your recording app both refuse it), Windows is using details it saved for an earlier firmware. Open Device Manager, choose View › Show hidden devices, and under Sound, video and game controllers uninstall every OpenGP5 and GP-5 Open FW entry (leave “delete the driver” unticked). Then unplug the pedal and plug it in again. Firmwares built before 1.0 have no USB audio. Their MIDI port is called GP-5 Open FW instead of OpenGP5.

body:
OpenGP5 is a small project that a few people work on in their spare time. Help by reporting clear steps, making focused changes or improving the docs.
Ways to help Try it on your pedal and tell us how it went. OpenGP5 has run on only a handful of GP-5s so far. The beta-testing checklist takes about an hour. A hardware report can describe passed checks as well as faults. Write a firmware. Start from the firmware template, then list it in the catalog so Launchpad and the web flasher can offer it. Report a bug with the bug form. Improve the platform or the docs with a pull request (below). Ask and answer questions in Discussions. Before you start on a change For a change beyond a fix or doc edit, open an issue or discussion. Describe what you want to change and why. The docs target platform 0.8.0-alpha and the planned 1.0 API. Discuss changes to public headers, callbacks, manifest fields or USB commands before writing them.
Pull requests Fork the repository, create a branch, and make one focused change. Run the tests on your computer. They need no pedal and no cross-compilers: tools/test_all.sh If you changed platform code, also build the examples for the pedal (release/setup-toolchain.sh once, then platform/build_firmware.sh tremolo). Continuous integration (CI) runs these checks on each pull request. Anything that changes how the pedal behaves needs a test on a real pedal before it’s merged. Say in the pull request whether you did one, and how: the maintainers may do it if you can’t. Keep pull requests to one change each, and describe what and why. How the code is written C99, no C library on either processor: the platform provides what’s needed (gp5_math.h, gp5_fmt.h). Nothing from the chip vendor’s SDK and nothing from Valeton: no code, headers, libraries, firmware or data. Code here is written from how the hardware behaves. A pull request that includes any of it can’t be merged. Comments explain why the code works this way. Use plain words and match the file’s style. For each new public call or callback, add a header comment and an entry in docs/platform/api.md. New host tests go into tools/test_all.sh. Docs Write for someone who has not worked with the pedal’s hardware.
Say what a tool does before explaining how it works. Use short sentences, active voice and plain words. Aim for a Flesch Reading Ease score of 80 or higher in prose. Remove adverbs and vague claims about ease, speed or safety. Keep a calm tone. Avoid sales language and buzzwords. Use technical terms when they help, and define them at first use. Put code names in backticks. Match button labels to the app. State whether an edit changes the live sound, saved settings or a preset. Keep version requirements and recovery limits consistent across guides. Licence OpenGP5 uses the MIT licence. If you send a pull request, you agree to share your work under that licence.
Conduct Be kind and assume good intent: see the code of conduct.

Dreamcatcher With Dreamcatcher on the pedal, Presets shows a live editor and 8 preset slots. Live editing needs version 1.2 or later. Tempo sync (Free / Sync and BPM) needs 1.4 or later. BPM means beats per minute.
Change and save the sound Turn a control in the live editor to hear the change. Changes made on the pedal also appear here. Use Save in the live editor to store the current sound in the active preset. Changing the live sound does not replace a saved preset until you save it.
Edit the preset slots Name a preset, move it left or right, or clear it. Export a preset to share it; Import loads one from a file. Click Write to pedal to save the edited slots. This replaces the pedal’s set of 8 presets. Undo changes discards the slot edits and returns to the set read from the pedal. Save or discard slot edits before using the live editor’s Save control. If Launchpad asks you to restart after writing, unplug and reconnect the pedal before saving a preset on it.
Valeton’s firmware With Valeton’s firmware on the pedal, Presets shows its 100 presets. Saving edits needs V1.0.6.
Select a preset. Edit the order of its effect blocks, the model and settings in each block, or its volume. Enable Hear it live to hear edits on the pedal. Click Save to pedal to store the preset. Undo changes discards the draft edits. Hearing an edit does not save it. Save before you switch presets or leave the page if you want to keep the change. You can also rename, reset, export or import one preset. After an import, click Save to pedal to store it.
Launchpad reads model names from a copy of Valeton’s firmware that it downloads on request. The app does not include that firmware or its data.
Clear a group of files Clean up the pedal can clear all 100 presets, all SnapTones or all user IRs. Read the confirmation and back up or export the data you want to keep before you clear it.

If a flash fails or the pedal doesn’t start The factory loader provides USB update mode. USB update tools cannot overwrite it. Try these steps to flash a working build:
Unplug the pedal. Press and hold the foot switch and the PARA knob. Keep both held as you plug the pedal back in, then release them. Check update mode. Launchpad or the web flasher should find the pedal in update mode. With the command-line tool, run python3 tools/gp5tool.py status. Use the tool’s status to confirm the mode; the screen alone is not a reliable check. Flash again. Choose a build that worked before, another build or Valeton’s firmware. When USB isn’t enough Some GP-5s have a fault in the DSP updater. The flash stops at the start of the DSP section with each tool. Valeton Suite may stop at 0 %. If the flash has written no DSP data, unplug the pedal and plug it back in. It should run its old build. A pedal stuck on BOOTLOAD may also need the steps below.
If a stalled flash leaves the pedal starting in update mode every time, you can get it running again over USB, without J7: gp5tool.py unstick installs Valeton’s firmware without the DSP section. See Pedal stuck in update mode for the command and what it erases. Flashes still stall after that, until the J7 fix below.
These pedals need an FT232H USB debug adapter wired to J7 inside the case to get past the fault. J7 recovery explains how to confirm the fault, flash OpenGP5, and apply the fix. Read that guide before opening the pedal.
Going back to Valeton’s firmware Use Launchpad or the command-line tool to flash Valeton’s firmware. If the DSP fault blocks the flash, use the J7 steps above.
With Launchpad: open Flash and choose Valeton’s firmware. Launchpad downloads V1.0.6 from Valeton’s site. Read the data notice and confirm the flash. Keep the pedal plugged in until it returns.
From the command line: download the GP-5 update from Valeton and unzip it. From your OpenGP5 folder, flash the full image, using the file’s path:
python3 tools/gp5tool.py flash GP-5_USB_V1.0.6_20250626.bin --sections all Use the name of the file you downloaded. Use one of the tools above to go back. Valeton Suite can fail when you try to return from OpenGP5.
The pedal starts with Valeton’s factory presets. To get your own presets back:
Open Launchpad’s Backups page and restore the backup you made before switching. Import any SnapTones and user IRs you exported in Valeton Suite. Without those backups and exports, flashing Valeton’s firmware does not restore your custom data.

The tremolo makes the guitar’s volume rise and fall with a wave. Use it to learn how an OpenGP5 effect handles settings, presets, the screen and controls. Your first effect builds a smaller version step by step.
Controls Control Action Turn PARA Select RATE, DEPTH, SHAPE or PRESET Press PARA Start editing the selected row; press again to finish Turn PARA while editing Change the value; on PRESET, load the selected slot Hold PARA for 0.6 s Save the sound in the displayed preset slot Press the foot switch Toggle the effect; mint LEDs mean on, dim red means off Turn the volume knob Set the output level RATE runs from 0.5 to 15 Hz. DEPTH sets how far the volume falls. SHAPE offers sine, triangle and square waves. There are four preset slots.
Bluetooth and MIDI Pair GP-5 over Bluetooth MIDI from a phone, a tablet or a Mac, or use the USB cable: the same MIDI works on both, on any channel.
MIDI Does Program Change 0–3 Loads presets 1–4 (an empty one is ignored) CC 20 Rate (0.5 … 15 Hz) CC 21 Depth CC 22 Shape (sine, triangle, square) CC 23 Tremolo off (0–63) or on (64–127) Launchpad works over Bluetooth too. Flashing needs the USB cable.
Get it Install the tremolo with the web flasher. To build it, set up your computer, then run these commands from the OpenGP5 folder:
platform/build_firmware.sh tremolo python3 tools/gp5tool.py flash build/GP-5_tremolo.bin --sections all Read Before you flash before writing to the pedal. The source is in firmwares/tremolo. Use Launchpad’s Live page to edit the installed tremolo’s settings.

body:
Build a tremolo from firmwares/passthrough. It makes the guitar’s volume rise and fall with a sine wave. Turn PARA to set the rate. Press PARA to switch between rate and depth. The foot switch toggles the effect. Launchpad uses your settings list to show an editor.
Complete the setup guide first. Run commands from the OpenGP5 folder. The sound and control code below totals about 90 lines. The full firmwares/tremolo example adds presets, more wave shapes and smooth text.
See the API reference for all calls. These docs target platform 1.0.0. The platform field below targets 1.0.
1. Copy the passthrough cp -r firmwares/passthrough firmwares/my-tremolo Then give it its own identity in firmwares/my-tremolo/firmware.json:
{ "id": "my-tremolo", "name": "My Tremolo", "version": "0.1.0", "author": "you", "platform": "1.0" } The id matters: the pedal’s storage belongs to the firmware with that id. Keep it once people use your firmware. A different id starts with empty storage.
The pedal has two processors, and a firmware has one part for each:
firmwares/my-tremolo/firmware.json who it is firmwares/my-tremolo/params.h its settings (you add this one) firmwares/my-tremolo/dsp/firmware.h the sound: runs on the DSP, 64 samples at a time firmwares/my-tremolo/nds32/firmware.c the knobs, foot switch and screen: runs on the control processor 2. The settings (params.h) Declare them once; both halves and the computer use the same list:
#define GP5_PARAMS(P, C) \ P(RATE, "Rate", "Tremolo", 50, 1500, 500, GP5_U_NONE, GP5_P_DSP | GP5_P_SAVE) \ P(DEPTH, "Depth", "Tremolo", 0, 100, 50, GP5_U_PERCENT, GP5_P_DSP | GP5_P_SAVE) \ C(ON, "Effect", "Tremolo", 2, "Off|On", 1, GP5_P_DSP) RATE runs from 50 to 1500 in 1/100 Hz, so 0.5 to 15 Hz. Values are whole numbers; choose the step you need. GP5_P_DSP means the DSP gets the value. GP5_P_SAVE means it is kept across power-off. ON has neither SAVE nor PRESET, so it starts at its default, on, after power-on. The platform now sends each change to the DSP, saves RATE and DEPTH 2 s after you stop turning, and lets a computer read and set all three. Parameters and presets has the units, flags and presets.
3. The sound (dsp/firmware.h) The platform calls:
static void fw_init(void); /* once, at start-up */ static void fw_process(const int32_t *in, int32_t *out_left, int32_t *out_right); /* every 1.45 ms */ static void fw_param(uint32_t id, int32_t value); /* a setting changed */ static int fw_command(uint32_t cmd, const uint8_t *payload, uint32_t n); /* commands of your own */ in holds GP5_BLOCK (64) guitar samples, 32-bit signed, full scale ±2^31. Divide by GP5_FULL_SCALE if you prefer -1.0 … 1.0. Write 64 samples to each output. Write ordinary C. Variables at file level keep their value between calls, and float maths runs on the DSP’s floating-point unit. gp5_math.h gives you sinf, cosf, expf, logf, powf, tanhf, sqrtf and more. Write 0.5f, not 0.5. A plain 0.5 is a double, which the DSP runs in software at a higher time cost. The build warns about it. Big buffers (delay lines, loopers) go in the 122 KB block: static int16_t line[44100] GP5_LARGE;. Ordinary variables have 19,712 bytes. The build prints what you use and refuses what doesn’t fit. gp5_param(GP5_P_DEPTH) reads a setting’s current value anywhere. Until the control half sends its values, it holds the defaults from params.h. Replace firmwares/my-tremolo/dsp/firmware.h with this:
/* My tremolo, DSP half */ #include "gp5_math.h" static float phase; /* 0 .. 1, one full wave */ static float step; /* phase per sample = rate / sample rate */ static float depth_now; /* the depth in use, gliding to the setting so changes never click */ static void set_rate(int32_t centi_hz) { step = (float)centi_hz / 100.0f / (float)GP5_SAMPLE_RATE; } static void fw_init(void) { phase = 0.0f; depth_now = 0.0f; set_rate(gp5_param(GP5_P_RATE)); } static void fw_param(uint32_t id, int32_t value) { if (id == GP5_P_RATE) set_rate(value); /* DEPTH and ON are read where they are used */ } static void fw_process(const int32_t *in, int32_t *out_left, int32_t *out_right) { float target = gp5_param(GP5_P_ON) ? (float)gp5_param(GP5_P_DEPTH) / 100.0f : 0.0f; for (uint32_t i = 0; i < GP5_BLOCK; i++) { depth_now += 0.001f * (target - depth_now); float wave = 0.5f + 0.5f * sinf(2.0f * GP5_PI * phase); /* 0 .. 1 */ float gain = 1.0f - depth_now * wave; phase += step; if (phase >= 1.0f) phase -= 1.0f; int32_t y = (int32_t)((float)in[i] * gain); out_left[i] = y; out_right[i] = y; } } static int fw_command(uint32_t cmd, const uint8_t *p, uint32_t n) { (void)cmd; (void)p; (void)n; return 0; } Use GP5_SAMPLE_RATE in the maths so the code works at either supported sample rate. The timing notes below explain the DSP’s cycle budget.
4. Try the sound on the computer No pedal needed:
python3 tools/run_effect.py my-tremolo guitar.wav out.wav --set Rate=400 --set Depth=100 python3 tools/run_effect.py my-tremolo x out.wav --tone # no recording? a plucked test tone --set sends a setting through the DSP’s parameter callback. The tool compiles your sound code for the computer with the platform’s maths functions. gp5_log("...") prints to the terminal.
After adding the control half in section 5, run python3 tools/simulate.py my-tremolo. The simulator then runs both halves, saves screen images and reads scripted controls.
5. The controls and screen (nds32/firmware.c) The platform calls these from its main loop. Each is optional, and none of them may wait:
function when the tremolo fw_init start-up (saved settings already loaded) fw_para_turn(clicks) PARA turned change the selected setting fw_para_click PARA pushed and let go select the other setting fw_foot_down foot switch pressed on / off fw_param_changed(id) a setting changed from the computer update the LEDs fw_draw(force) every pass the screen The volume knob sets output level by default. Replace firmwares/my-tremolo/nds32/firmware.c with this:
/* My tremolo, control half: PARA turn = the selected setting, PARA click = select, foot = on / off */ #include "gp5_firmware.h" #include "gp5_params.h" static unsigned sel; /* 0 = rate, 1 = depth */ static void show_on(void) { gp5_led(gp5_param(GP5_P_ON) ? GP5_LED_ON : GP5_LED_BYPASS); } void fw_init(void) { show_on(); } void fw_foot_down(void) { gp5_param_set(GP5_P_ON, !gp5_param(GP5_P_ON)); show_on(); } void fw_param_changed(unsigned id) { if (id == GP5_P_ON) show_on(); } void fw_para_click(void) { sel = !sel; } void fw_para_turn(int d) { if (sel == 0) gp5_param_set(GP5_P_RATE, gp5_param(GP5_P_RATE) + 10 * d); /* 0.1 Hz a click */ else gp5_param_set(GP5_P_DEPTH, gp5_param(GP5_P_DEPTH) + 5 * d); /* (clamped to the range) */ } static void number(char *p, unsigned v, unsigned digits) /* right-aligned decimal */ { for (unsigned i = digits; i-- > 0; v /= 10) p[i] = (char)('0' + v % 10); } int fw_draw(int force) { static int32_t shown[3] = { -1, -1, -1 }; static unsigned shown_sel = 9; int32_t rate = gp5_param(GP5_P_RATE), depth = gp5_param(GP5_P_DEPTH), on = gp5_param(GP5_P_ON); if (force) { gp5_text(0, "My Tremolo "); gp5_text(4, " "); shown[0] = shown[1] = shown[2] = -1; } if (rate != shown[0] || sel != shown_sel) { char s[14] = " rate 00.00Hz"; if (sel == 0) s[0] = '>'; number(s + 6, (unsigned)rate / 100, 2); number(s + 9, (unsigned)rate % 100, 2); gp5_text(1, s); shown[0] = rate; } if (depth != shown[1] || sel != shown_sel) { char s[14] = " depth 000 %"; if (sel == 1) s[0] = '>'; number(s + 8, (unsigned)depth, 3); gp5_text(2, s); shown[1] = depth; } if (on != shown[2]) { gp5_text(3, on ? " on " : " off "); shown[2] = on; } shown_sel = sel; return 0; } The screen here is five lines of 13 characters (gp5_text). For smooth text in any font and size, see Text and fonts; for your own pixels, gp5_blit. firmwares/tremolo draws its rows that way.
6. Build, check, flash python3 platform/manifest.py firmwares/my-tremolo --check # is firmware.json right? platform/build_firmware.sh my-tremolo # -> build/GP-5_my-tremolo.bin python3 tools/dsp_emu_check.py build/GP-5_my-tremolo.bin # boots the built DSP code in an emulator (pip install unicorn) python3 tools/gp5tool.py flash build/GP-5_my-tremolo.bin --sections all You can also flash it from Launchpad or the web flasher. Both read the name and version from the file.
On the pedal:
python3 tools/gp5_link.py params # your settings and their values python3 tools/gp5_link.py set Depth 100 # change one from the computer python3 tools/gp5_link.py log -f # what gp5_log() prints, on either processor python3 tools/gp5_link.py status # how busy both processors are Launchpad’s Live page shows your settings as knobs and switches.
For a pedal that does not start, follow Recovery. That guide covers entering update mode and the DSP fault that can block a USB flash.
7. Make it yours Presets: add "presets": 4 to firmware.json, and GP5_P_PRESET instead of GP5_P_SAVE on the settings that make a sound. gp5_preset_load(n) / gp5_preset_save(n) from your controls; Launchpad can load, save and rename them too. firmwares/tremolo uses PARA hold to save (Parameters and presets). A settings page: the UI kit draws a page of your parameters and handles PARA for you, in about ten lines. firmwares/tremolo uses it. Your own text for a value: GP5_U_CUSTOM and fw_param_text(), so the screen and Launchpad say “5.00 Hz”. More sound: a drive (tanhf), a filter (a biquad is 5 multiplies per sample), an echo (a GP5_LARGE buffer), a chorus (a short delay whose length follows a slow sinf). 8. Next steps firmwares/tremolo: this tremolo finished, with presets, a smooth-font screen that redraws only what changed, PARA click and hold, and a screen preview that runs on the computer (test/screen.sh). The audio link ("audio": {"link": true}, gp5_link_start) exchanges words between the halves after every block. Use it for data that changes all the time, or to run sound on the control chip too. NAM Loader runs most of its model there this way. Dreamcatcher: a large firmware in its own repository, with a looper, delays, reverb, presets and a graphic screen, built on OpenGP5 as a submodule. Timing notes At 44.1 kHz, one 64-sample block gives the DSP about 278,000 cycles at 191.9 MHz. That is about 4,300 cycles per sample. At 48 kHz, the budget drops to about 255,900 cycles per block. A sinf call costs about 40 cycles; this tremolo uses a few percent of a block. Measure the built effect on the pedal before adding more work. See Performance.

body:
This changelog tracks the OpenGP5 platform. NAM Loader and Dreamcatcher have their own release notes. From 1.0, no 1.x release breaks a firmware written for 1.0 (see Versions in the API reference).
Each entry says what changed in that release. Use the current guides to set up the tools or fix a failed flash.
1.0.0: USB audio, Bluetooth MIDI, a stable API Set "platform": "1.0" in firmware.json. Firmwares written for 0.7 or 0.8 build unchanged; they get USB audio only with "usb_audio": true.
New The pedal is a USB audio interface. Class-compliant, two channels each way, 16-bit, at the firmware’s sample rate, next to USB-MIDI; no driver on macOS or Windows (Linux should need none either: not yet tested). The computer records the firmware’s finished output and can play through the pedal’s outputs. On by default for firmwares written for 1.0; "usb_audio": false turns it off. A firmware that finishes its sound on the control processor (NAM Loader) uses "usb_audio": {"record_from": "control"} and gp5_usb_audio_record(). See USB audio in the API reference. Direct sound off while the computer plays. A DAW monitoring the pedal would otherwise be heard twice: once straight from the pedal, once back from the DAW. Launchpad’s pedal panel, gp5_link.py direct off, or the firmware (gp5_usb_audio_set_direct()) leave the pedal’s own sound out of the outputs while the computer plays into the pedal. Recording doesn’t change; with nothing playing, the pedal is always heard; back on after a restart. Bluetooth MIDI, per firmware. With "bluetooth": true the pedal advertises as OpenGP5 with the BLE-MIDI service. Notes, controllers, program changes and real-time messages (MIDI clock, start, stop) reach the new fw_midi() hook, from USB as well. Launchpad, the phone remote and gp5_link.py work over it; flashing needs USB. The radio and BLE code are OpenGP5’s own. More room for firmwares. The platform’s own buffers moved to RAM the platform didn’t use before, so a firmware now has 264,160 bytes of control-processor RAM (was 258,016), promised for all of 1.x. Pedals whose updates stall. gp5tool.py tickfix applies the 4-byte fix to the DSP updater; gp5tool.py unstick gets a pedal out of update mode without J7; tools/j7_nudge.py and the J7 recovery guide get the first OpenGP5 firmware onto such a pedal. Changed The pedal is called OpenGP5 over USB (was GP-5 Open FW), for the MIDI port and the audio device, and over Bluetooth (was GP-5). Launchpad 0.4, the web flasher and gp5tool.py find both names. Older versions of those tools don’t see a pedal running a 1.0 firmware, except in update mode, which is still called GP-5. Documentation A documentation website, opengp5.github.io: getting started, Launchpad, each firmware, building your own, help; the web flasher moved to /flasher/ (the old address still works). New pages: USB audio, the phone remote, J7 recovery, the DSP updater fault (help wanted: a USB-only route to its fix), the colour palette. Fixed The audio link recovers from more stalls. Restarting it now clears every DMA flag, not only “done”; a latched error had kept some links dead through every restart. The crash record survives a watchdog restart. It was in memory that read as noise on most firmwares. gp5_ms() keeps time on heavy firmwares. It lost milliseconds while an audio-link handler ran for over 1 ms (up to 23 % slow on NAM Loader); it now catches up from the cycle counter. 0.8.0-alpha: the UI kit, the simulator, the template Set "platform": "0.8" in firmware.json when using a feature added in this release. Code for 0.7 still builds, apart from the older 0.6 API and GP5_DATA described under Removed.
Fixed The audio link restarts after a stall. Some builds never started an exchange at power-on. The fault depended on code layout; its cause was not found. The main loop now rearms the link after 50 ms without an exchange. It logs audio link: no exchange …. The sound on message reports the exchange count. A test that stopped the link on purpose recovered within 50 ms. Audio waits for saved settings at start-up. The platform used to turn sound on when the DSP answered, then send settings one every 20 ms. That could play default settings or dry guitar during start-up. It now sends settings back to back, with a three-second limit, before fading sound in. Output level also glides across its full range over 23 ms to avoid clicks. Flashing waits through macOS MIDI reconnect errors. The tool keeps waiting if MIDI port listing fails while the pedal restarts. It retries the first update-mode query up to four times. Thanks to dk55432, issue #3. New MIDI tools retry RtMidi -304. If the macOS MIDI service is not ready, gp5tool.py, gp5_link.py and gp5_data.py retry up to three times before sending data. After a send begins, they stop and report the error. The UI kit provides reusable screen tools. gp5_ui.h adds a settings page, value text (gp5_param_format), messages and knob pickup. Turn PARA to select a row; press it to edit. An optional row selects presets. Pickup waits until the knob reaches the saved value before it takes control. Unused kit code adds no bytes to an image. See docs/platform/ui.md. Launchpad’s Developer page shows logs and load. It reads the pedal’s log, processor load and memory for builds on platform 0.7 or later. The UI kit adds menus. gp5_ui_menu_t lets PARA select actions and a press run them. Items marked for confirmation ask “Sure?” before a second press. Items can show a value, such as the target preset. The tremolo uses the settings page and menu. Turn PARA to select a row, then press it to edit. Earlier controls used a press to change rows and a turn to change values. The tremolo’s square wave avoids abrupt edges. Each edge glides over 5 ms. The tremolo version is 1.1.0, and the web flasher offers that build. Run both halves on your computer. tools/simulate.py runs the audio link with normal or early timing. A script drives the controls. The tool keeps saved settings and writes screen PNGs and sound WAVs. Use --check to find memory faults. It runs the tremolo, Dreamcatcher and NAM Loader. See docs/platform/simulator.md. Start your own project from a template. OpenGP5/firmware-template is an overdrive with settings, presets and the UI kit. It pins a copy of OpenGP5 as a submodule. Use build.sh to build it and test.sh to run the checks. GitHub Actions tests each push and publishes tagged builds. A dev container lets you build in GitHub Codespaces. Continuous integration checks builds and tests. .github/workflows/ci.yml runs tools/test_all.sh, builds the examples for the pedal and compares the web flasher’s tremolo with the source build. Linux and macOS builds match byte for byte. The catalog lists firmware builds and reserves IDs. Submit one catalog/ listing per firmware through a pull request. CI downloads each release and checks its checksum and metadata. tools/catalog.py manages listings; docs/catalog.json supplies the list to the apps. Launchpad and the web flasher read the catalog. Each checks file size, checksum and image details against the listing. Builds from other authors carry Not reviewed, which does not imply a source review. Shared catalog code lives in web/flasher/catalog.js. New files explain how to take part. Read CONTRIBUTING.md for ways to help and the code of conduct for the rules. Forms cover bugs, hardware reports and feature requests. A pull-request template lists the details to include. New guides explain the shared code. Read how it works, how the chips share sound work and how to measure load. Other guides cover finding bugs, sharing builds, common questions and known limits. Use BETA-TESTING.md to test your pedal. The code samples were built and run on a computer. DSP code can run from RAM. Mark per-sample functions with GP5_FAST. Use GP5_CYCLE_COUNT() to read the cycle counter on either chip. Control-chip on_block code can use GP5_BLOCK for the block size. The link-word limit is 264. That was the largest tested count without dropouts. The build no longer enables fused multiply-add, since that instruction hangs the control chip. Check how much screen data each pass sends. The simulator reports the largest transfer. Long transfers make controls and USB wait. Removed (the last planned breaking changes before 1.0) The 0.6 API. Every firmware folder now needs firmware.json. Removed callbacks are fw_foot, fw_foot_release, fw_para_push, fw_para_release, fw_knob, fw_level, fw_active, fw_draw(knob, force) and fw_store_changed. The manifest replaces these settings from dsp/firmware.h: GP5_AUDIO_LINK, GP5_LINK_WORDS, GP5_SAMPLE_RATE, GP5_CTL_MHZ and GP5_LINK_EARLY. GP5_DATA. The raw area from before 0.4 is gone. Use files through gp5_file. Preparing the 1.0 compatibility checks compat/1.0 holds example fixtures from 0.8 sources, pending the final 1.0 freeze. tools/test_compat.sh runs them in the simulator, and CI builds them for the pedal. The parameter test reads the saved fixture platform/nds32/test/params-1.0.store.hex. compat/1.0/budget.json caps the platform’s share of memory. CI checks it with tools/check_budget.py. See known-limits.md for the planned 1.x firmware budgets. GP5_DEPRECATED(instead) marks a call for retirement and warns during a build. The planned USB rules add reply fields at the end. Readers skip bytes they do not know. See protocols.md. The simulator now stops the build if a call has no declared function. This catches removed or renamed calls that used to cause a warning. 0.7.0-alpha: the 1.0 API This release introduced the planned 1.0 API. In 0.7, a build without firmware.json could still use the 0.6 API. Platform 0.8 removed that older path.
New firmware.json, a firmware’s manifest: id, name, version, author, licence, and what it needs (sample rate, audio link, 320 MHz, presets). It replaces the #defines in dsp/firmware.h and fw_name(). The build checks it (platform/manifest.py --check) and puts it in the image, so Launchpad, the web flasher and gp5tool.py info <file.bin> know what a .bin is before it is flashed. The pedal says what it runs too (USB 7E 16, gp5_link.py info). Parameters (params.h, docs/platform/params.md): declare the settings once, with name, group, range, default, unit and flags. The platform sends changes to the DSP (fw_param, gp5_param), keeps them across power-off, and lets a computer list, read and set them. Saved values survive firmware updates that add, remove or reorder parameters. Presets: "presets": N in firmware.json. The platform keeps them, with names: gp5_preset_load, _save, _rename, _current, _dirty. USB 7E 17; gp5_link.py presets. New control callbacks: fw_foot_down / fw_foot_up, fw_para_down / fw_para_up, fw_para_click and fw_para_hold (0.6 s), fw_tick (every 10 ms), fw_draw(force), fw_storage_changed. Platform calls gp5_knob, gp5_ms, gp5_led, gp5_level_own / gp5_level_set. gp5_log on both chips: printf-style lines with the time, read with gp5_link.py log -f. DSP lines travel over the link. gp5_fmt.h is the small printf behind it. gp5_link.py status: cycles per block (last and worst), the main loop’s longest pass, late blocks and memory in use, for both chips (USB 7E 14). run_effect.py --set Name=value, choices by name (--set Shape=Square); gp5_log prints to the terminal. The tremolo (firmwares/tremolo) is the example firmware, on the 1.0 API: parameters, four presets, a smooth-font screen, PARA click and hold, a screen preview on the computer. Docs: docs/platform/api.md (everything a firmware can use), docs/platform/params.md, the first-effect walkthrough rewritten for 1.0, the new USB and link commands in protocols.md. Changed Link command 0x7F10 carries parameters for a firmware with params.h; its own commands start at 0x7F11. The DSP’s load report (0x7F04) also gives memory in use, and can clear its peak readings. The hand-over to update mode (11 6F, flashing without Foot + PARA) always goes through a restart. It failed now and then for firmwares without the audio link. Removed The strobe tuner demo. The screen can’t refresh fast enough for a proper strobe. Upgrading a 0.6 firmware Add firmware.json. Use the name your fw_name() returned as id, so the pedal keeps its storage. Move GP5_SAMPLE_RATE, GP5_CTL_MHZ, GP5_AUDIO_LINK, GP5_LINK_WORDS and GP5_LINK_EARLY from dsp/firmware.h into it. Rename the callbacks: fw_foot → fw_foot_down, fw_para_push → fw_para_down, fw_draw(knob, force) → fw_draw(force) with gp5_knob(). Replace fw_knob with gp5_knob() or fw_tick, and fw_active with gp5_led(). Replace fw_level with gp5_level_own(1) + gp5_level_set(), if you set the level yourself. Optional, recommended: move the settings into params.h. fw_take, fw_setting_count, fw_dsp_ready and your 0x7F10 handling then go away, and Launchpad gets an editor for your firmware. NAM Loader 1.2 and Dreamcatcher 1.3 are ported examples. 0.6.0-alpha 320 MHz on the control chip, for heavy firmwares. 48 kHz audio (0.5.6). Fixed: slow preset loads and clicks after long flash writes; the DSP no longer stops answering after flash writes; LEDs stuck on red. 0.5.5-alpha Fixed clicks while a computer talks to the pedal: the DSP queues its replies. 0.5.4-alpha Storage as files, owned by the installed build (300 KB). Live settings from a computer (fw_param_get / fw_param_set, USB 7E 10 / 7E 11). The controls over USB (7E 0F). gp5_math.h on both chips. Audio link size per firmware. 0.2.x-alpha Storage across power-off (gp5_store_save / _load). LED colours. Switch releases. Smooth text (make_font.py). Firmwares in their own repositories. Reading the flash over USB. 0.1.0-alpha The first public release includes the shared code, passthrough, tremolo and grain delay.

body:
Live shows settings that an OpenGP5 build describes through its parameter API, added in platform 0.7. It also works with builds that Launchpad has no built-in editor for. The firmware supplies each setting’s name, range, unit and choices. Launchpad uses that list to show controls.
NAM Loader uses Tones and Dreamcatcher uses Presets, so Launchpad hides Live for those builds.
Change a setting Drag a knob or scroll over it. The sound changes as you play. Double-click a knob to return it to its default value. Click a choice button to select that value. The firmware decides which settings to keep after power-off. Settings marked for saving persist about two seconds after the last change. Other settings return to their defaults at power-on.
Load and save presets If the firmware defines presets, Live shows Load, Save and name fields. Load recalls a saved sound. Save stores the current sound in that slot and replaces any sound it held. An edit to the live sound does not replace the saved preset until you click Save. Editing a name saves the new name on the pedal.
For firmware authors Declare settings in params.h to show them here. See Parameters and presets for the save flags and API versions for the 1.0 API.

Use the firmware template to start your own GitHub repository. It contains an overdrive with drive, tone, level and four presets. Change that effect to make your own.
Start On the template’s page, click Use this template and create your repository.
Edit firmware.json to set id, name, author, url and description. The ID owns your firmware’s storage. Keep it after release so updates can find saved data.
Build it, in the browser or on your computer:
In the browser: choose Code › Codespaces › Create codespace. Wait for setup to finish, then run ./test.sh and ./build.sh in its terminal.
On your computer: install the required tools. In the commands below, replace <your repository> with your clone URL in the first line and folder name in the second:
git clone --recursive <your repository> cd <your repository> opengp5/release/setup-toolchain.sh # once ./test.sh # the whole firmware in the simulator ./build.sh # -> build/GP-5_<id>.bin Flash build/GP-5_<id>.bin with Launchpad, the web flasher or gp5tool.py.
What’s in it File Purpose firmware.json Who it is and what it needs (manifest) params.h Its settings: saved, in presets, sent to the DSP, editable from Launchpad (Parameters) dsp/firmware.h The sound, on the DSP: fw_process() gets 64 samples at a time nds32/firmware.c The controls and the screen, with the UI kit test/controls.txt What ./test.sh does in the simulator opengp5/ A Git submodule: a copy of OpenGP5 pinned to one release The submodule keeps platform code separate from your effect. Its pinned release records the code you built against. To update it, run git -C opengp5 checkout <tag> with the release tag you want. Test and commit the new submodule revision.
Built and released by GitHub GitHub Actions builds and tests each push. Find the image and screen previews under the run’s Artifacts. Push a tag such as v1.0.0 to publish a release with the image. Then list it in the catalog.
Licence The template uses the MIT No Attribution licence. Choose a licence for your firmware and put its name in firmware.json.

A backup is one .gp5backup file with the installed build’s supported data. It does not include a firmware installer. Check the table to see what it holds:
Firmware A backup holds NAM Loader Captures, cab IRs, IR choices, gate and EQ settings Dreamcatcher Presets Firmware with the parameter API, added in platform 0.7 Saved settings, presets and files Valeton’s firmware The 100 presets Launchpad cannot back up Valeton SnapTones or user IRs. Export those in Valeton Suite before you switch firmware. Valeton’s global settings stay on the pedal.
Back up Open Backups. Click Back up now and save the file. Check Backups from this computer to find saved backups. Restore Install the firmware that the backup came from. If the pedal runs a different one, flash it first. Select a backup in the list, or click Open a file. Tick the parts you want to restore, then click Restore and confirm. Restart the pedal if Launchpad asks you to do so. Restoring replaces the selected data on the pedal. Launchpad checks that the backup belongs to the installed build.
Before switching firmware A different firmware starts with empty storage. If Launchpad can read the pedal, it offers Back up first when you switch. Choose that option before you start the flash if you want to keep the old data.

OpenGP5 is for people at any skill level. Give others room to ask, try and share.
Expected conduct Give new users time to learn. Treat all users with care. Start from the view that others mean well. Talk about the code or idea. Keep the focus on the work. Name the people whose work you use. Unacceptable conduct Do not harass or insult people. Do not attack people. Do not discriminate against any group. Do not post sexual content. Do not share someone else’s personal details. Do not keep disrupting the space.
Do not post files that belong to Valeton or the chip vendor under copyright. Do not help others get those files. These rules apply to issues, pull requests, Discussions and the firmware catalog.
Report a problem Use Report content on the GitHub comment or user profile to report it to GitHub in private. You can reach the project in public on Discussions. Keep private details out of public posts. The team keeps reports private.
Enforcement The team may edit or remove posts, warn users, or block them from the project. It removes catalog listings that break these rules.
The Contributor Covenant helped shape these rules.

Something went wrong Problem Where to look A flash failed, or the pedal does not start Recovery Launchpad cannot access MIDI Click Restart Launchpad in its banner; see Connect The browser cannot find the pedal Use Chrome, Edge or Opera on a computer and allow MIDI access; see Web flasher Presets or captures disappeared after a flash A different firmware starts with empty storage; reinstall the matching firmware and restore its backup I want Valeton’s firmware back Going back My own effect has a fault Debugging Read the FAQ for common questions. Report a problem Open a GitHub issue in the project that has the fault:
OpenGP5: the platform, flash tools, web flasher and recovery. Launchpad: the desktop app. NAM Loader or Dreamcatcher: the effect. Give enough detail for someone to repeat the fault:
what you did, in order; what you expected and what happened; the effect name and version; the version of the shared platform code, if known; the app or flash-tool version and your system, such as macOS or Windows; the error text or log output. body:
tools/simulate.py runs both halves of a build on your computer. It has no live window. It reads a control script and saves screen images and sound files. It covers:
both chips’ code; the audio link between them; the screen, saved as pictures; the controls, from a script; guitar in and sound out as WAV files. You need Python and a C compiler (cc), but no pedal or cross-compilers. Install Pillow with pip install pillow if you want screen images. From the OpenGP5 folder, run:
python3 tools/simulate.py tremolo --script controls.txt --in guitar.wav --out out.wav Without --in it plays a plucked test tone for 4 s. Screens go to build/sim/<id>/ (end.png is the screen at the end) and the sound to build/sim/<id>.wav.
A script One line per action, the time in seconds first:
# the tremolo: faster, saved into preset 2, then bypassed 0.2 shot start 0.5 para click # adjust RATE 0.6 para turn 10 # +1.0 Hz 0.8 para click 1.0 para turn 3 # down to PRESET 1.1 para click 1.2 para turn 1 # P2 1.4 para hold # held 0.8 s: saves at 2.0 s 2.1 shot saved 2.5 foot 3.0 set Shape Square # as a computer sets it 3.2 knob 128 Script action Meaning foot press and let go of the foot switch (foot down / foot up: one edge) para click, para hold push PARA and let go after 0.1 s / 0.8 s (para down / para up: one edge) para turn N turn PARA N clicks (negative: back) knob N the volume knob, 0..255 set NAME VALUE a parameter, as Launchpad sets it: by the name shown (Loop_level for “Loop level”) or the code’s (LOOPLV); a choice by its name preset load N, preset save N presets, numbered from 1 as on the pedal shot NAME the screen now, as NAME.png storage changed as when a computer changed the firmware’s files While it runs, it prints the log (gp5_log on either processor, the DSP’s lines marked dsp:) and every LED change. At the end, the tool reports the largest screen update from one fw_draw call. On the pedal, that transfer takes time in a main-loop pass. Draw a strip at a time to leave room for other work. OpenGP5 examples send up to about 8 KB of the 25.6 KB screen in a pass. The tool reports the first full draw as a separate value.
More options Option Meaning --seconds S how long (default: the input’s length) --knob N where the volume knob starts (default 255) --store FILE keep saved settings and presets in FILE between runs, as the pedal keeps them across power-off --files DIR the firmware’s files (gp5_file): every file in DIR, by its name --check build with the address and undefined-behaviour checkers: a crash or a bad memory access stops with the file and line it happened on --shots DIR, --out WAV where screens and sound go How close is it to the pedal? The same:
The firmware’s own code, both halves. The platform’s parameters, presets, UI kit, text drawing and maths (gp5_math.c), so the arithmetic is the pedal’s. The timing: 64-sample blocks, fw_tick every 10 ms, the PARA hold at 0.6 s, the order of the main loop, and the audio link’s words arriving three blocks on (both normal and link_early exchanges). Different:
Speed is not simulated. Code that is too slow for the pedal runs fine here: measure with gp5_link.py status on the pedal. GP5_CYCLE_COUNT() and the control chip’s cycle counters read 0. The DSP-extension instructions of the control chip (kmmac and friends) don’t exist on a computer. Code that uses them needs a portable version for when __NDS32_EXT_DSP__ isn’t defined (NAM Loader’s kernel has one). Saved data lives in memory or the --store file, not flash, so flash timing and wear don’t apply. Controls are exact: no bounce, no noise on the knob. Use the simulator to check sound and screen code after a change. You can also run it in continuous integration (CI), the build and test process that runs on each push. Check speed and control feel on the pedal.
How it works platform/host/sim_dsp.c builds the DSP half as a library, and platform/host/sim.c is the control half’s main program with the platform’s calls. They are kept apart because each half has its own fw_init, sinf and so on. tools/test_simulate.py checks the simulator itself.
