A mod changes part of Valeton’s V1.0.6 firmware. Launchpad downloads a copy from Valeton, checks the bytes the mod will change, and flashes the result.
Install or undo a mod With Valeton V1.0.6 on the pedal, open Mods. Read the mod’s description and click Install. Let Launchpad download and check Valeton’s firmware, then read and confirm the change. Keep the pedal connected until the flash finishes. To undo the mods, click Restore Valeton’s original under Undo mods. When the pedal runs Valeton’s firmware, a mod or undo keeps its presets. If you switch from OpenGP5, back up first. That switch clears the old data.
USB audio interface, no direct monitoring This mod sends the sound from your recording app to the pedal’s outputs. Your app must send the guitar sound back over USB for you to hear it from those outputs. If the app sends no sound back, the outputs stay silent.
The USB recording channels stay the same:
Channels Signal sent to the computer 1 and 2 Dry guitar 3 and 4 The processed preset Undo the mod to use the pedal on its own.
Load a mod file Click Open a mod file and choose a .gp5mod file. Read its description, then click Install. Launchpad checks the original bytes before it applies each change. Those checks confirm that the patch fits; they do not review what the mod does.

body:
Declare your firmware’s settings in params.h. The platform uses that list to:
send DSP-marked values when they change and after a DSP restart; keep values marked SAVE or PRESET across power-off; keep named presets if the manifest defines slots; let a computer read and change values. Launchpad uses the list to build its Live editor. Parameter support began in platform 0.7, with the 1.0 API.
Your control code can read and set these values. The UI kit supplies a settings page that lets users select and edit them with PARA.
Declaring them params.h, at the top of the firmware’s folder (next to firmware.json):
#define GP5_PARAMS(P, C) \ P(RATE, "Rate", "Tremolo", 50, 1500, 500, GP5_U_CUSTOM, GP5_P_DSP | GP5_P_PRESET) /* 1/100 Hz */ \ P(DEPTH, "Depth", "Tremolo", 0, 100, 50, GP5_U_PERCENT, GP5_P_DSP | GP5_P_PRESET) \ C(SHAPE, "Shape", "Tremolo", 3, "Sine|Triangle|Square", 0, GP5_P_DSP | GP5_P_PRESET) \ C(ON, "Effect", "Tremolo", 2, "Off|On", 1, GP5_P_DSP) P(id, name, group, min, max, default, unit, flags) a number, min..max, within -32768..32767 C(id, name, group, count, "A|B|C", default, flags) a choice, 0..count-1 Each line gives an id, GP5_P_RATE, GP5_P_DEPTH and so on (0, 1, 2 …, in order), and GP5_NPARAMS counts them. Names and groups have at most 15 characters; a choice list at most 47. Launchpad shows each group as a card.
Values are whole numbers from -32,768 to 32,767, kept as 2 bytes in saved settings and presets; this range is fixed for all of 1.x. Pick the step the user needs and say it in the unit: 1/100 Hz for a rate, ms for a time, tenths of a dB for a gain. Something that needs more (a length in samples, say) is better stored in a coarser unit, or as two parameters.
Units How a computer shows a value:
unit shown as GP5_U_NONE the number GP5_U_PERCENT 50 % GP5_U_DB10 tenths of a dB: -60 → −6 dB GP5_U_MS 350 ms, 1.5 s GP5_U_HZ 440 Hz GP5_U_SEMITONES +7 st GP5_U_CENTS10 tenths of a cent GP5_U_CUSTOM your own text: fw_param_text() on the control chip writes it (below) Flags Flag Effect GP5_P_DSP the DSP gets it: fw_param(id, value) there, and gp5_param(id) GP5_P_PRESET part of a preset; also kept across power-off as part of the current sound GP5_P_SAVE kept across power-off on its own: a global setting, not part of presets GP5_P_READONLY the computer may read it, not set it: a state such as “looping” or the note played GP5_P_HIDDEN not shown in Launchpad’s editor A parameter with neither PRESET nor SAVE starts at its default after every power-on (the tremolo’s ON).
Control processor #include "gp5_params.h" void fw_para_turn(int d) { gp5_param_set(GP5_P_DEPTH, gp5_param(GP5_P_DEPTH) + 5 * d); } void fw_foot_down(void) { gp5_param_set(GP5_P_ON, !gp5_param(GP5_P_ON)); } gp5_param(id): the current value. By fw_init() the saved values are already in place. gp5_param_set(id, value) sets a value from your control code. It clamps the value to its range and sends it to the DSP if marked GP5_P_DSP. For SAVE or PRESET values, it schedules a save two seconds after the last change. It returns 1 if the value changed. The delay reduces flash writes while the user turns a knob. fw_param_changed(id) (optional): a value changed from outside, either from the computer or from a preset load (once per parameter that changed). Redraw, or update the LEDs. It is not called for your own gp5_param_set. fw_param_text(id, value, text) (optional): for GP5_U_CUSTOM, write up to 15 characters and return 1. The computer asks for it (USB 7E 15), so your screen and Launchpad show the same thing: int fw_param_text(unsigned id, int32_t v, char *t) /* RATE: 500 -> "5.00 Hz" */ { if (id != GP5_P_RATE) return 0; ... return 1; } DSP static void fw_param(uint32_t id, int32_t value) { if (id == GP5_P_RATE) step = (float)value / 100.0f / (float)GP5_SAMPLE_RATE; } The platform keeps every DSP parameter’s value; gp5_param(id) reads it anywhere, including in fw_process. The platform calls fw_param before the next audio block. Use it to compute filter coefficients, delay lengths or other values that need extra work. Read small values where you use them. The DSP starts with defaults from params.h until the control chip sends the saved values.
Link command 0x7F10 carries parameters; a firmware’s own link commands start at 0x7F11.
Presets "presets": N in firmware.json (up to 64). A preset holds every GP5_P_PRESET parameter and a name of up to 12 characters.
Call Result or action gp5_preset_count() N gp5_preset_load(n) 0 if preset n is empty (nothing changes); otherwise every value, then fw_param_changed for each one that changed gp5_preset_save(n) the current sound into n, keeping its name gp5_preset_current() the preset loaded last, -1 if none gp5_preset_dirty() 1 once the sound differs from that preset (show a *) gp5_preset_used(n) Check whether slot n holds a saved sound gp5_preset_name(n) Read slot n’s name gp5_preset_rename(n, name) Change slot n’s saved name The platform saves the current preset number with the current sound. Your firmware chooses the controls: the tremolo loads on the PRESET row and saves on a PARA hold. Launchpad can load, save and rename presets through the same API. Changing the current sound does not overwrite a saved preset until you call gp5_preset_save(n).
How they are stored In the firmware’s own storage (storage.md), as store records whose ids come from the firmware’s id: one for the current sound, one for each preset. A record keeps pairs of (a hash of the parameter’s name, value), not positions, so an update that adds, removes or reorders parameters keeps what was saved:
a new parameter starts at its default; a removed one is dropped; a renamed one starts at its default (keep names once released). Ranges are applied when values are loaded.
Launchpad includes these records in a backup. Restoring them returns the saved presets and current sound. Keep the firmware ID and parameter names stable so the records still match.
Firmware ids past the parameters A firmware can answer more live ids, starting from GP5_NPARAMS, with fw_param_get / fw_param_set: commands or states that aren’t settings. Dreamcatcher does this for its own preset commands. The platform passes it every id it doesn’t own.
Trying it python3 tools/run_effect.py tremolo x out.wav --tone --set Rate=800 --set Shape=Square python3 tools/gp5_link.py params python3 tools/gp5_link.py set Depth 80 python3 tools/gp5_link.py presets

Use Developer to read the pedal’s log and check the work each chip does. It needs firmware built on platform 0.7 or later.
The pedal’s log Messages from gp5_log on either processor appear as the pedal sends them. Pause stops the display from scrolling. Save writes the displayed log to a file. See Debugging for ways to use the log.
Load and memory Load is the share of one 64-sample audio block that a task takes to run. Last shows the most recent block; worst shows the peak since the last reset. The DSP is the digital signal processor that handles the audio.
Display Meaning Audio block Time the DSP takes to process a block Audio-link handler Time the control chip spends on audio, if the build uses the audio link Main loop, longest pass Longest pass through the control chip’s screen, controls and USB work, shown as a share of a block RAM, Variables, GP5_LARGE buffers Memory in use and the limit for each area Keep peak audio load below about 85 % on both chips while using the settings that use the most time. The main-loop bar measures response time for controls; it is not an extra audio task to add to those loads.
Click Reset worst to clear the peak readings and start a new measurement. See Performance for timing limits and ways to reduce load.

body:
The UI kit in platform/nds32/gp5_ui.h provides screen and control tools built on parameters. Use the pieces you need. Unused kit code takes no space in the built image. Dreamcatcher, for example, draws its own screen.
Tool Purpose gp5_param_format() a value as text, the way Launchpad shows it gp5_ui_page_t a settings page: a row per parameter, PARA picks and adjusts gp5_ui_page_message() a short message in the page’s last row gp5_ui_menu_t a menu of actions: PARA picks, a click runs one, risky ones ask “Sure?” first gp5_pickup_t Knob pickup: wait until the knob reaches the current value before it takes control A settings page #include "gp5_ui.h" #include "fonts/sans_16.h" static const uint8_t rows[] = { GP5_P_RATE, GP5_P_DEPTH, GP5_P_SHAPE, GP5_UI_PRESETS }; static gp5_ui_page_t page = { .rows = rows, .n = 4, .font = &gp5_font_sans_16, .row_h = 20, .upper = 1 }; void fw_para_turn(int d) { gp5_ui_page_turn(&page, d); } void fw_para_click(void) { gp5_ui_page_click(&page); } int fw_draw(int force) { return gp5_ui_page_draw(&page, force); } How it works on the pedal:
Turn PARA to pick a row. The row picked is highlighted, and the page scrolls when there are more rows than fit. Press PARA to adjust it. A bar on the left and < > around the value show you’re adjusting. Turning now changes the value; press PARA again to finish. Numbers stop at their range, choices go round, and read-only parameters can’t be adjusted. The presets row (GP5_UI_PRESETS, if the manifest has "presets") shows P2 name, with * when the sound differs from it. Adjusting it loads presets as you turn; empty ones are shown but not loaded. Saving is the firmware’s choice of control. The tremolo saves on a PARA hold: void fw_para_hold(void) { if (gp5_preset_save(gp5_ui_page_preset(&page))) gp5_ui_page_message(&page, "Saved", 1500); } What you can set (leave anything else 0 for its default):
Field Meaning rows, n the rows: parameter ids and GP5_UI_PRESETS. Without rows, every parameter that isn’t GP5_P_HIDDEN, then the presets steps per row, how much one click changes it. Default: about 1/50 of the range, rounded to 1, 2, 5, 10, 20 …; values stay on that grid font required: a font your firmware includes (fonts.md) row_h row height; default the font’s line height. sans_16 with 20 px rows gives 4 rows; sans_12 with 16 px gives 5 y, h the part of the screen the page uses (default: all of it), e.g. below a header you draw yourself title a title row at the top upper labels in capitals theme colours: { bg, ink, dim, accent, on_accent } as 0xRRGGBB; default dark grey, white and teal faded set to 1 to grey the values out, e.g. while the effect is bypassed; the page redraws when it changes gp5_ui_page_draw draws one changed row per call and returns non-zero while more are left, like any fw_draw. Return that result from your fw_draw. The page also shows changes from preset loads and the computer. Use gp5_ui_page_row() to find the selected row if your screen needs more detail.
A menu A menu lists actions such as save, reset and back. Turn PARA to select an item, then press PARA to run it. For an item marked confirm, the menu asks “Sure?”. Press PARA again to confirm. Turn away or wait three seconds to cancel. An item’s value() shows text on the right, such as the target preset.
The tremolo’s page with a menu on a PARA hold (it runs as it is in the simulator):
static const uint8_t rows[] = { GP5_P_RATE, GP5_P_DEPTH, GP5_P_SHAPE, GP5_UI_PRESETS }; static gp5_ui_page_t page = { .rows = rows, .n = 4, .font = &gp5_font_sans_16, .row_h = 20, .upper = 1 }; static int in_menu, switched; /* switched: draw everything once after a switch */ static void close_menu(void) { in_menu = 0; switched = 1; } static void save(void) { if (gp5_preset_save(gp5_ui_page_preset(&page))) close_menu(), gp5_ui_page_message(&page, "Saved", 1500); } static void reset(void) { for (unsigned id = 0; id < GP5_NPARAMS; id++) gp5_param_set(id, gp5_param_table[id].def); close_menu(); gp5_ui_page_message(&page, "Reset", 1500); } static const char *save_slot(void) /* the preset "Save" writes to: the one the page shows */ { static char t[4] = "P1"; t[1] = (char)('1' + gp5_ui_page_preset(&page)); return t; } static const gp5_ui_item_t items[] = { { "Save", save, save_slot, 0 }, { "Reset all", reset, 0, 1 }, /* asks for a second click */ { "Back", close_menu, 0, 0 }, }; static gp5_ui_menu_t menu = { .items = items, .n = 3, .font = &gp5_font_sans_16, .row_h = 20, .upper = 1, .title = "MENU" }; void fw_para_turn(int d) { if (in_menu) gp5_ui_menu_turn(&menu, d); else gp5_ui_page_turn(&page, d); } void fw_para_click(void) { if (in_menu) gp5_ui_menu_click(&menu); else gp5_ui_page_click(&page); } void fw_para_hold(void) { in_menu = !in_menu; switched = 1; if (in_menu) gp5_ui_menu_pick(&menu, 0); } int fw_draw(int force) { if (switched) { force = 1; switched = 0; } return in_menu ? gp5_ui_menu_draw(&menu, force) : gp5_ui_page_draw(&page, force); } Item field Meaning label the item’s name run called on a click (or the second click, with confirm); 0 for an item that only shows something value optional: a function returning the text on the right; asked whenever the menu draws, so it can change confirm 1: ask “Sure?” first The menu takes the same font, theme, title, y, h, row_h and upper as the page. gp5_ui_menu_message() shows a message in its last row, gp5_ui_menu_pick() picks an item (the first, say, when the menu opens) and gp5_ui_menu_item() says which is picked.
Value text char t[16]; gp5_param_format(GP5_P_TIME, gp5_param(GP5_P_TIME), t); /* "350 ms", "1.50 s" */ The formatter shows choice names and the same units as Launchpad: 50 %, -6 dB, +5.5 dB, 440 Hz, +7 st. For GP5_U_CUSTOM it asks your fw_param_text(), so the screen and Launchpad always agree.
Knob pickup A physical knob may point to a different value from the saved setting. Use pickup to wait until the knob crosses the saved value before it takes control. This avoids a jump when you load a preset or give the knob a new task:
static gp5_pickup_t knob; void fw_init(void) { gp5_level_own(1); gp5_level_set(255); gp5_pickup_start(&knob, GP5_P_MIX); } void fw_tick(void) { gp5_pickup_poll(&knob); } The value stays fixed until the knob crosses it. The knob then controls the whole range. Call gp5_pickup_start again after a preset load or when assigning another setting. Call gp5_level_own(1) to stop the knob from also changing output level. This helper waits for a value crossing; Dreamcatcher’s own control code uses a movement threshold instead.
Trying it without a pedal python3 tools/simulate.py <firmware> --script s.txt runs your page and menu with scripted controls and saves the screens (simulator). firmwares/tremolo/test/screen.sh runs the tremolo’s control half on the computer, presses its controls and saves each screen as a PNG, kit and all. Copy it for your own firmware. platform/nds32/test/ui_test.sh tests the kit itself.

The screen is 160 × 80 pixels. Use the built-in pixel font or draw smooth text with a font header. You can also convert your own font to a header.
1. The built-in pixel font: gp5_text gp5_text(2, "rate 5.00 Hz"); /* line 0..4, up to 13 characters, white on black */ gp5_text draws five lines of up to 13 characters. It supports printable ASCII, including lowercase. The 5×7 font draws at double size and needs no setup. Use it for settings, status or debugging. The source is petabyt’s font, under the MIT licence, in platform/nds32/font5x7.h.
2. Smooth text in any font: gp5_text_at and gp5_draw_text #include "gp5_font.h" #include "fonts/sans_24.h" gp5_text_at(4, 10, &gp5_font_sans_24, "Delay", 0xFFFFFF, 0x101820); /* straight to the screen */ gp5_text_at(x, y, font, text, colour, background) draws a line on the screen. x, y is the top-left corner. Colours use 0xRRGGBB. gp5_draw_text(buffer, w, h, x, y, font, text, colour) draws into your own pixel buffer. It blends text over the existing pixels. Use the screen format that gp5_blit accepts, then send the buffer with that call. The tremolo draws this way, one row at a time (firmwares/tremolo/nds32/firmware.c). gp5_text_width(font, text) measures, for centring or right-aligning. A font knows its line height (font->h) and where its baseline is (font->base, pixels below the top). The platform includes sans, based on Atkinson Hyperlegible Next. It uses weight 600 (semibold). Choose a size from fonts/sans_12.h, sans_16, sans_20, sans_24, sans_32 or sans_40. The number is the pixel size; line height is about a third larger. A build includes the sizes you use. Size 12 takes about 3 KB; size 40 takes about 26 KB.
The source font supports weights from 200 (extra light) to 800 (extra bold). Its file is platform/nds32/fonts/AtkinsonHyperlegibleNext-VariableFont_wght.ttf. For a bold title, run:
python3 tools/make_font.py platform/nds32/fonts/AtkinsonHyperlegibleNext-VariableFont_wght.ttf font_title 24 \ firmwares/my-effect/nds32/font_title.h --weight 800 \ --notice "Atkinson Hyperlegible Next, SIL Open Font License 1.1 (LICENSE-AtkinsonHyperlegibleNext-OFL.txt)" 3. Your own font Use make_font.py to turn a TrueType (.ttf), OpenType (.otf) or BDF (.bdf) font into a header. This does not need a platform change:
pip install pillow python3 tools/make_font.py MyFont.ttf font_title 28 firmwares/my-effect/nds32/font_title.h \ --notice "MyFont, Copyright 20xx The MyFont Authors, SIL Open Font License 1.1" #include "font_title.h" gp5_text_at(4, 4, &font_title, "My effect", 0xFFFFFF, 0x000000); 28 is the size in pixels for a TrueType font. For a BDF font it is the scale instead: 1 copies it pixel for pixel, 2 doubles every pixel (crisp, for pixel-art looks). --chars "0123456789.-+%" keeps only the characters you list; the others take no room. A big readout font then costs a fraction of a full one. --weight W picks a variable font’s weight. The tool rejects values outside that font’s range. --notice adds a notice to the header. See the licence notes below. Make as many sizes as you need; each is its own header. Font licences Keep the font’s copyright and licence notice in the header. Put its licence file beside the header. Read the font’s own terms for conversion and sharing. For a font under the SIL Open Font License (OFL), check whether it lists a Reserved Font Name. A modified font may need a new name.
Preview text Use firmwares/tremolo/test/screen.sh as a screen-preview example. It runs the same drawing code on your computer and saves PNG files so you can check the text before flashing.

body:
The installed build owns the pedal’s saved data. A build with a different ID starts with no data. An update with the same ID keeps it. If you rename a setting, that setting can reset to its default.
Back up before switching. Launchpad offers a backup when it can read the running firmware. A backup belongs to the firmware that made it; install that firmware before you restore the data.
Who owns it Before fw_init(), the platform reads GP5O, the record of who owns the data. It checks that record against the string id in firmware.json:
If the ID matches, the platform keeps the data. If another ID owns the area, the platform clears it and marks it with the new ID. If the area has no mark, the platform keeps the data and adds the mark. Older builds used fw_name() to claim storage. Since 0.5.3, the default name opengp5 does not claim storage. A mark with that default name from 0.5.2 counts as no mark. This lets a later named build keep that data.
Launchpad also clears storage when switching firmware. From a running OpenGP5 build, it does this before flashing. From Valeton’s firmware, it clears the area after the new build starts. Back up before you start, since a flash failure does not undo a storage erase.
Returning to Valeton Launchpad clears the shared area and writes Valeton’s preset-order table at 0x170000. The table is 100 bytes, numbered 0 through 99. Without it, Valeton’s firmware can refuse to save presets.
Valeton then shows its factory presets. Restore your preset backup to get your saved presets back. Import exported SnapTones and user IRs in Valeton Suite; Launchpad cannot back them up.
The map (control processor flash) Flash Size What 0x000000–0x00FFFF 64 KB factory loader (USB updates leave it in place) 0x010000–0x13EFFF ≤ 1.2 MB the firmware’s code (OpenGP5 builds 60–110 KB; Valeton’s 1.2 MB) 0x13F000–0x15FFFF 132 KB files, run A (33 sectors) 0x160000–0x161FFF 8 KB settings (gp5_store) 0x162000–0x189FFF 160 KB files, run B (40 sectors). 0x170000–0x189FFF is Valeton’s user-preset area when Valeton’s firmware is installed 0x190000–… Valeton’s factory presets, models, global settings (0x1D0000): outside the platform storage area The shared storage spans 0x13F000–0x189FFF, about 300 KB. Storage-write commands cannot write outside that range.
Settings: small, saved often Use gp5_store_save(id, data, len) and gp5_store_load(id, …) for records up to 1 KB. These records suit presets, options and the last selected item. The store appends records to a log across two 4 KB sectors to spread flash wear.
Files: larger data Use files for captures, samples and IRs that a computer writes. Each file has a numeric firmware ID and a name of up to 31 ASCII characters, such as tone-03. This numeric file ID is separate from the firmware’s string ID in firmware.json.
A file occupies whole 4 KB sectors, in one consecutive run. There are 73 file sectors across two runs. The firmware can read the data from flash without copying the whole file into RAM.
Each file starts with a 64-byte header. Data starts at offset +64:
Offset Size Field 0 4 magic GP5F (0x46355047) 4 4 sequence number: the newest copy of a firmware id + name wins 8 4 firmware id 12 4 data length in bytes 16 4 CRC-32 (zlib) of the data 20 2 sectors the file occupies (header + data) 22 2 flags, 0 24 32 name, ASCII, zero-padded 56 4 CRC-32 of bytes 0–55 60 4 0xFFFFFFFF Write, delete and read files The computer writes a new copy in this order:
Find and erase a free run of sectors. Write the data, then write the header last. Read the new file back to check it. Erase the first sector of the old copy, if one exists. Writing the header last lets readers reject an incomplete new copy after a power cut. Deleting a file erases its header sector. Firmware reads files with gp5_file(), gp5_file_check() and gp5_file_each().
After you write files or settings, send 7E 0E <id>. The platform reads the saved settings and presets, then calls fw_storage_changed() to load other data.
Backups A format 2 backup names the build it came from. It saves that build’s files, settings and presets. The app rejects a backup from a different build, or one that lacks a build ID. It checks the ID again while it holds the pedal link for the restore.
A backup holds data, not a firmware installer. See Launchpad Backups for the supported data types.

body:
The audio link exchanges 32-bit words between the two chips after each audio block. A word is one 32-bit value. Send guitar samples to the control chip, process them there, and read the result on the digital signal processor (DSP).
The control chip can suit code that needs more time or memory:
it has a 264,160-byte firmware RAM budget, compared with the DSP’s 19,712 bytes plus 122,880 bytes; it ran the same float code about 1.7 times faster; with its integer DSP instructions, fixed-point code is much faster again (performance). NAM Loader runs most of its amp model there. Dreamcatcher runs its whole engine there and mixes on the DSP.
The result returns three blocks later: about 4.4 ms at 44.1 kHz or 4 ms at 48 kHz. Keep the dry path on the DSP to avoid adding this round-trip delay to it.
The smallest example The guitar goes to the control chip, gets a soft clip there, and comes back.
firmware.json: ask for the link and how many words each way:
{ "id": "link-demo", "name": "Link demo", "version": "0.1.0", "platform": "1.0", "audio": { "link_words": 64 } } dsp/firmware.h:
static void fw_init(void) {} static void fw_process(const int32_t *in, int32_t *out_left, int32_t *out_right) { const int32_t *back = gp5_link_in(); /* the control processor's words: a block from 3 blocks ago, processed */ int32_t *to = gp5_link_out(); /* words for the control processor */ for (uint32_t i = 0; i < GP5_BLOCK; i++) { to[i] = in[i]; out_left[i] = out_right[i] = back[i]; } } static int fw_command(uint32_t cmd, const uint8_t *p, uint32_t n) { (void)cmd; (void)p; (void)n; return 0; } nds32/firmware.c:
#include "gp5_firmware.h" #include "gp5_math.c" /* sinf, tanhf ... for this processor (once per firmware) */ static void on_block(const int32_t *in, int32_t *out) /* in an interrupt, once per block: keep it short */ { for (unsigned i = 0; i < GP5_BLOCK; i++) { float x = (float)in[i] / 2147483648.0f; out[i] = (int32_t)(tanhf(4.0f * x) * 0.5f * 2147483647.0f); } } void fw_init(void) { gp5_link_start(on_block); } Try it: python3 tools/simulate.py <folder>. The simulator runs the link with the pedal’s timing.
How it works After each block, the DSP sends link_words words and receives as many. The platform frames them with a sync word and finds them again on the other side; you only see your words. On the control chip, on_block(in, out) runs in an interrupt once per block. in holds the DSP’s words. What you write to out goes back to the DSP. On the DSP, gp5_link_out() takes the words for the control chip during fw_process(), and gp5_link_in() has what came back. Words from the control chip reach fw_process() 3 blocks after the block they were made from. Rules and limits link_words: a multiple of 8, up to 264. The build rejects larger values. Measured at 48 kHz, 264 words worked; 296 caused dropouts. An exchange takes about 38 % of a block per 128 words. Pack data if you need more values. NAM Loader packs 24-bit samples in block floating point (pack24.h in its repository). link_early: use this if fw_process() takes more than about half a block. Set "audio": { "link_words": N, "link_early": true }, with your word count in place of N. The exchange starts at the start of each block using the previous block’s output. Define static void fw_link_early(const int32_t *in, int32_t *out) on the DSP. The platform calls it before the exchange, so it can put new input into out. NAM Loader uses this path. on_block must finish within a block (1.45 ms; 1.33 ms at 48 kHz). It interrupts the main loop, so the longer it takes, the less time is left for the screen and USB. gp5_link.py status shows its share: keep the worst under about 85 %. Don’t call the platform from on_block. No drawing, no storage, no gp5_param_set. Hand data to the main loop through variables; gp5_log is allowed but costly. A lost exchange repeats or skips a block. Rare, but a long flash write (saving, a computer writing files) can cause it. If your data has state (a model’s history, a sequence), put a counter in a word and check it on the other side, as NAM Loader and Dreamcatcher do. Who does what: patterns that worked Firmware DSP work Control-processor work Dreamcatcher dry signal, final mix, reverb, exact bypass the whole looper / delay / grain engine (float) NAM Loader the model’s first layers, bypass the remaining layers, the cab IR (fixed point), gate, EQ Measure both sides with gp5_link.py status while playing your heaviest settings.

body:
The DSP must finish fw_process() within each 64-sample block. A block lasts 1.45 ms at 44.1 kHz or 1.33 ms at 48 kHz. If you use the audio link, the control chip must also finish on_block() within that time. These figures come from measurements on the pedal. Measure your effect under load to check that it fits.
The budgets Processor Cycles per block at 44.1 kHz At 48 kHz DSP (191.9 MHz) about 278,000 about 255,900 control processor at 288 MHz 417,920 384,000 control processor at 320 MHz ("control": {"mhz": 320}) 464,384 426,624 Keep peak load below about 85 % of a block on each chip. Peak load is the most time used by any measured block. Test with the settings that use the most time so the spare time covers changes in load.
Measuring Run python3 tools/gp5_link.py status with the pedal connected. It shows current and peak block load, late blocks, the longest main-loop pass, and memory. Late blocks can cause audible glitches. Add --reset to clear the peak readings. Launchpad’s Developer page shows the same readings.
Time a piece of code with GP5_CYCLE_COUNT() on either processor. Keep its peak cycle count. Log that value once per second to limit the log’s own time cost:
static volatile uint32_t worst; /* the slowest block so far, in cycles */ static void on_block(const int32_t *in, int32_t *out) { uint32_t t = GP5_CYCLE_COUNT(); /* ... the work ... */ t = GP5_CYCLE_COUNT() - t; if (t > worst) worst = t; } void fw_tick(void) /* every 10 ms: report once a second */ { static unsigned n; if (++n % 100 == 0) gp5_log("worst %lu cycles of %lu", (unsigned long)worst, (unsigned long)(GP5_CTL_MHZ * 1000000u / GP5_SAMPLE_RATE * GP5_BLOCK)); } Read it with gp5_link.py log -f.
The simulator and run_effect.py don’t count cycles: they check what your code computes, not how fast it is.
The DSP Average about 4 to 5 cycles per instruction, even from RAM. A trivial loop step measured 32 cycles. Budget per sample, not per block: 278,000 cycles per block is about 4,300 per sample.
Code runs from flash unless you say otherwise, and big loops miss its small fetch cache. Dreamcatcher’s audio loop took 110 % of a block from flash and 42 % from RAM. Mark the functions that run for every sample with GP5_FAST:
GP5_FAST static void fw_process(const int32_t *in, int32_t *out_left, int32_t *out_right) { ... } This code shares the 19,712-byte variable area. Use it for loops that run often and cost the most time. Measured 2026-11-25 (cycles per float multiply-add): a small loop takes 13 from flash and 24 with GP5_FAST; 5 KB of straight-line code takes 10 from flash and 12 with GP5_FAST. So keep small loops in flash, and use GP5_FAST for large loops with branches, which miss the flash cache. The build may then warn about a “LOAD segment with RWX permissions” because the section holds code in writable RAM.
float, never double. The float unit is single precision; double runs in software and is many times slower. Write 0.5f, not 0.5 (the build warns about doubles).
Maths functions cost tens of cycles (sinf about 40; powf, expf and tanhf more). Work out what you can in fw_param(), when a setting changes, not per sample: a filter’s coefficients, a delay length, a gain in decibels turned into a factor. For a waveform, a phase accumulator and sinf, or a small table, are both fine.
Put large buffers in the 122,880-byte area with GP5_LARGE. The measured access speed is the same for both RAM areas.
The control chip Its float unit takes about 5 cycles per operation, with no overlap. Even so, the same float code ran about 1.7 times faster than on the DSP, and it has more memory.
It has no working fused multiply-add. The instruction exists, but it hangs the processor. The platform’s build never uses it; don’t turn it on with your own compiler flags.
Its integer DSP instructions run about one per cycle: __nds32__kmmac_u, __nds32__kmmawb_u / _kmmawt_u (32 × 16 bits), __nds32__kwmmul_u, from <nds32_intrinsic.h>. Fixed-point code built on them is several times faster than float.
NAM Loader’s float cab IR used about 5 cycles per float operation: 256 taps took 9 % of a 48 kHz block, and 1,024 taps didn’t fit. Rewritten in fixed point with these instructions, 1,024 taps fit with the whole amp model (worst 79 % of a block at 320 MHz). Keep a portable version of such code for when __NDS32_EXT_DSP__ isn’t defined, so the simulator can run it.
Code runs from flash through a cache, built for small size (-Os). A file with hot code can ask for speed with #pragma GCC optimize("O2") at its top, as NAM Loader’s a2.c does.
Choose 320 MHz with "control": {"mhz": 320}. This matches Valeton’s clock and gives about 11 % more cycles per block.
The main loop Your callbacks (fw_draw, fw_tick and controls) share the main loop with USB and saving. A long pass delays controls and USB. Audio runs in interrupts, but long flash writes can still disrupt the audio link. gp5_link.py status shows the longest pass. Aim for one or two blocks per pass:
draw the screen in strips (fw_draw returns non-zero while more is left), not all at once. The simulator says how much your firmware sends in one pass: NAM Loader’s passes of 13-18 ms came from sending 14 KB at once, and strips of a quarter of the screen fixed them; move heavy work out of callbacks, or spread it over several passes; saving to flash takes about 1 ms, and a few hundred ms now and then (an erase). The platform saves parameters 2 s after the last change for you. When it doesn’t fit In this order:
Measure first: which part is slow? Move calculations that depend on a setting, such as filter coefficients, into fw_param(). Put the most time-consuming DSP loops in RAM (GP5_FAST). Move work to the other processor over the audio link. On the control chip, rewrite the most time-consuming loop in fixed point. Run part of it at half rate: Dreamcatcher’s reverb runs at half rate on the DSP, in about 36 % of a block.

body:
Use the simulator to find bugs before you flash the pedal. On the pedal, use the log and load report to find faults.
On the computer Tool What to check python3 tools/simulate.py <fw> --script s.txt --check Run both halves with checks for memory errors and undefined behavior python3 tools/run_effect.py <fw> in.wav out.wav Run the DSP sound code and listen to its output python3 tools/dsp_emu_check.py build/GP-5_<id>.bin Boot the built DSP image in an emulator and check replies, output level and sound gp5_log("...") Print log lines from either half while the simulation runs Replace <fw> with the firmware folder or name, and <id> with its manifest ID. Use a control script that exercises the changed behavior. See The simulator. Run --check after changes to memory use or control flow. The checks can point to the source line of a fault. They do not measure whether the code meets the pedal’s timing budget.
On the pedal python3 tools/gp5_link.py log -f # gp5_log lines from both processors as they come (the DSP's marked "dsp:") python3 tools/gp5_link.py status # how busy both processors are, late blocks, memory python3 tools/gp5_link.py info # which firmware and platform it runs python3 tools/gp5_link.py params # every parameter's value python3 tools/gp5_link.py stats # the link to the DSP: frames, errors Launchpad’s Developer page shows the log, processor load and memory for platform 0.7 or later. Use Reset worst to clear peak readings before a test. Copy or save the log to include it in a bug report.
gp5_log uses printf-style formatting. It accepts %d %u %x %s %c %f, widths and precision such as %.2f. Print uint32_t as %lu with an unsigned long cast. The pedal keeps the last 4 KB of log text; new text overwrites old text if the reader falls behind.
Log once per second or on an event. A log line in every block adds load and can affect the test. The platform also logs its start-up: the build name, clock and DSP memory.
Symptoms Symptom Check Next action Full red LEDs A main-loop callback may have blocked for more than two seconds Remove waiting loops; read status for the longest pass Silence DSP reply, output level and audio-link start Read status, log and params; check the volume knob Clicks or crackles Late blocks, lost audio-link exchanges or abrupt gain changes Measure load while playing; smooth gain changes Zipper noise when turning a knob A value may jump once per block Smooth the value per sample Slow controls or screen A long main-loop pass Draw less per pass; see Performance Settings lost after power-off Save flags and firmware ID Check GP5_P_SAVE / GP5_P_PRESET and firmware.json Black screen and no USB device A start-up crash Follow recovery below, then use the simulator’s --check RtMidi -304 on macOS MIDI service readiness Wait, reconnect the pedal and retry if the tools’ three retries fail For silence, check whether status says DSP did not answer. If the firmware owns output level, gp5_level_set(0) mutes it even when the knob is up. An audio-link effect also needs gp5_link_start() to run its control-processor handler.
For zipper noise, a per-sample glide such as x += 0.002f * (target - x) can smooth a changing value. Choose the smoothing time to suit the setting. The tremolo’s square-wave code is another example.
After a MIDI error, tools retry if they have sent no data. Once a send has started, they stop and report the fault.
Recovery USB update tools leave the factory loader in place, so a crashed app does not erase that recovery path.
Unplug the pedal. Press and hold the foot switch and PARA as you plug it back in, then release both. Confirm update mode with Launchpad, the web flasher or gp5tool.py status. Flash a build that worked before. See Recovery for the full steps. The known DSP updater fault can still block a USB flash; J7 recovery covers that case. If that stall leaves the pedal starting in update mode every time, gp5tool.py unstick gets it running over USB, without J7: see Pedal stuck in update mode.
The same firmware ID keeps storage. A different ID starts with empty storage, so back up before switching.
Asking for help Open a Discussion, or an issue for a fault in OpenGP5. Include:
the steps that trigger the problem; what you expected and what happened; output from gp5_link.py info, status and log; a control script that reproduces it, if you can make one.

body:
To share a build, give it a version, publish the image and add it to the catalog. Users can then find it in Launchpad and the web flasher.
Before the first release Start a repository with the firmware template. Choose your own id in firmware.json. Do not release with the template’s my-effect ID. Keep your ID after release: changing it starts users with empty storage. Claim the ID in the catalog. You can submit a listing before adding releases. Add a LICENSE file and name the licence in firmware.json. Choose setting names you can keep. A saved value uses the setting’s name as its key. A rename gives that setting its default value. You can add, remove or reorder other settings without resetting names that still match. A release 1. Set the version Update version in firmware.json:
Change Example Fix 1.0.0 → 1.0.1 New feature that keeps compatibility 1.0.0 → 1.1.0 Incompatible change 1.0.0 → 2.0.0 Test release 1.1.0-beta.1 2. Pin the platform Use the OpenGP5 release you tested. Check it out in the opengp5 folder, for example git -C opengp5 checkout v1.0.0. Set platform in your manifest to the release’s major and minor number, such as "1.0". Commit the pinned copy with your changes.
3. Test the build Run ./test.sh to check scripted controls in the simulator, then ./build.sh to make the image. On a pedal, check these cases:
Play with the settings that use the most time while gp5_link.py status reports load. Power off and on. Check that saved settings return. Update from your last release. Check that saved data still loads. 4. Tag and publish Make a tag that matches the version with git tag v1.0.1, then push it with git push origin v1.0.1. The template uses GitHub Actions to build the image and put GP-5_<id>.bin on your Releases page. It also runs tests on each push. This is continuous integration (CI).
5. Update the catalog Add the release to catalog/<id>.json in OpenGP5, newest first. Run python3 tools/catalog.py release GP-5_<id>.bin <download-url> to print a listing from the image. Use your build’s filename and download link in the command.
Run python3 tools/catalog.py check, then python3 tools/catalog.py index. Open a pull request with the listing changes. CI downloads the image and checks it against the listing.
Writing the release notes Tell users:
what changed and which faults the release fixes; whether settings and presets carry over, including any renamed settings or changed IDs; which pedal and software versions you tested; how to install the previous release and where to find the recovery steps. Tell users about the known DSP update fault. It can block a USB flash, so link to the steps for that case.
Good practice Build from a clean copy of the release tag. The template’s CI uses that source so users can check the same build. Keep old builds in the catalog so users can go back. Handle bugs in your effect in its own project. Report faults in the shared code to OpenGP5.

body:
This page lists the public calls, callbacks and manifest fields. Read each header’s comments for full call details. An API is the set of calls and commands your effect can use. These docs target platform 1.0.0. See Versions for the distinction. Start with How a firmware works, then use these guides: parameters, UI kit, audio link, performance, debugging, simulator, releasing, storage, fonts, questions.
Header Processor Purpose platform/nds32/gp5_firmware.h control (NDS32) callbacks, controls, screen, LEDs, storage, log, audio link platform/nds32/gp5_font.h control smooth text in any font (Fonts) platform/nds32/gp5_ui.h control the UI kit: a settings page, a menu, value text, messages, knob pickup (UI kit) platform/dsp/gp5_dsp.h DSP (Cortex-M4F) fw_init, fw_process, fw_command, log, audio link, cycle counters platform/dsp/gp5_params.h both parameters and presets (Parameters) platform/dsp/gp5_math.h both sinf, expf, logf, tanhf, … (neither processor has a C library) platform/dsp/gp5_fmt.h both a small printf (gp5_log uses it) Each firmware folder needs firmware.json. The build rejects a folder without it. Platform 0.8 removed the older 0.6 API, which allowed builds without a manifest.
A firmware’s folder my-effect/ firmware.json who it is and what it needs (below) params.h its parameters (optional; params.md) dsp/firmware.h the sound: fw_init, fw_process, fw_command, fw_param (gp5_dsp.h) nds32/*.c screen and controls: fw_draw, fw_foot_down, ... (gp5_firmware.h) Keep your effect under firmwares/, or put it in your own Git project with a pinned copy of OpenGP5. Git calls that copy a submodule. In that case, pass your effect folder’s path to the build.
The firmware template sets this up. GitHub Actions tests and builds each push. A tag can publish a release. You can also build in a browser with GitHub Codespaces. See firmwares/tremolo for a full example.
firmware.json { "id": "tremolo", "name": "Tremolo", "version": "1.0.0", "author": "OpenGP5", "url": "https://github.com/OpenGP5/OpenGP5", "licence": "MIT", "description": "The volume rises and falls.", "platform": "1.0", "presets": 4 } Field Required? Meaning id required lowercase letters, digits and -, up to 31. It names the firmware’s storage: a firmware with another id starts with empty storage, so keep it once released name required shown by Launchpad and the web flasher version required 1.2.0 or 1.2.0-beta.1 author, url, licence, description optional shown by Launchpad (Version / By on the Pedal page) platform optional the API version it was written for, major.minor; the build refuses a newer minor or another major presets optional how many presets the platform keeps for it, 0..64 (Parameters) audio.sample_rate optional 44100 (default) or 48000 audio.link optional true: the audio link between the processors (below) audio.link_words optional 32-bit words each way per block: a multiple of 8 from 8 to 264 (200 while USB audio records from the DSP); default 128; enables link audio.link_early optional start the exchange at the beginning of each audio block; define DSP fw_link_early (see below) control.mhz optional 288 (default) or 320: the control chip’s clock (11 % more cycles) bluetooth optional true: Bluetooth MIDI (below): the pedal advertises as OpenGP5, MIDI reaches fw_midi, the computer’s commands work over it usb_audio optional the pedal as a USB audio interface (below): on by default with "platform": "1.0" or later, off for older firmwares unless true; false turns it off; {"record_from": "control"} for a firmware that finishes its sound on the control processor Run python3 platform/manifest.py <folder> --check to validate the fields. Use your firmware folder’s path. The build creates definitions for both chips: GP5_FW_ID, GP5_SAMPLE_RATE, GP5_CTL_MHZ, GP5_AUDIO_LINK, GP5_LINK_WORDS, GP5_PRESETS, GP5_HAS_PARAMS, GP5_BLUETOOTH and GP5_USB_AUDIO (with USB audio also GP5_LINK_TOTAL, GP5_USB_PLAY_AT, GP5_USB_REC_AT or GP5_USB_RECORD_CONTROL).
The image stores the manifest with its code, in a metadata block. The tools read it to show the build’s name and version before a flash. Run gp5tool.py info <file.bin> to read a file. The pedal sends the same details through USB command 7E 16.
Control processor: what the platform calls You can omit these callbacks. The platform uses an empty function in their place. They run in the main loop, so do not wait for events inside them. A blocked loop turns the LEDs full red after two seconds. See Performance for shorter response-time targets.
Callback When it runs void fw_init(void) once at start-up, after the storage claim and the saved parameters are loaded int fw_draw(int force) every pass: draw part of the screen with gp5_blit; return non-zero while more is left. force = draw everything void fw_tick(void) every 10 ms void fw_foot_down(void) / fw_foot_up the foot switch, debounced (30 ms) void fw_para_down(void) / fw_para_up the PARA knob pushed / let go void fw_para_click(void) a push let go within 0.6 s (just before fw_para_up) void fw_para_hold(void) a push held 0.6 s (once, while still held; no click follows) void fw_para_turn(int detents) PARA turned, + clockwise void fw_param_changed(unsigned id) a parameter changed from outside: the computer, a preset load (Parameters) int fw_param_text(unsigned id, int32_t v, char *text) the text of a GP5_U_CUSTOM value, up to 15 characters void fw_storage_changed(void) the computer changed this firmware’s files or records: read them again void fw_midi(const uint8_t *msg, unsigned n) a MIDI message from USB or Bluetooth, status byte first, from the main loop: a note, controller, program change, pressure or pitch bend (n = 2 or 3), or a real-time byte (n = 1): clock 0xF8 (24 a beat), start 0xFA, continue 0xFB, stop 0xFC, active sensing 0xFE, reset 0xFF. Check the status byte and n. SysEx is the platform’s int fw_param_get/fw_param_set(uint32_t id, ...) the firmware’s own live ids past its parameters (Dreamcatcher’s preset commands) Control processor: what a firmware may call Call Result or action gp5_knob() the volume knob, 0..255, filtered gp5_ms() milliseconds since start GP5_CYCLE_COUNT() the core’s cycle counter, for timing code (performance) gp5_level_own(1), gp5_level_set(0..255) take over the output level (by default the volume knob sets it) gp5_led(GP5_LED_ON / GP5_LED_BYPASS / GP5_LED_RGB(r, g, b)) the LEDs: mint (default), dim red, or a colour (0..32 each) gp5_blit(x, y, w, h, px) pixels to the 160 × 80 screen (gp5_color(0xRRGGBB) makes one) gp5_text(line, s) the built-in 5×7 font, 5 lines of 13 characters gp5_draw_text, gp5_text_at, gp5_text_width smooth text (gp5_font.h, Fonts) gp5_param, gp5_param_set, gp5_preset_* parameters and presets (Parameters) gp5_ui_page_*, gp5_ui_menu_*, gp5_param_format, gp5_pickup_* the UI kit (UI kit) gp5_store_save(id, p, len) / gp5_store_load(id, p, max) a record of up to 1 KB, kept across power-off (Storage) gp5_file, gp5_file_check, gp5_file_each files the computer wrote (captures, IRs): read straight from flash gp5_log(fmt, ...) a line for the log (below) gp5_link_start(on_block) start the audio link (below) Bluetooth To send MIDI over Bluetooth, set "bluetooth": true. The pedal uses Bluetooth Low Energy MIDI (BLE-MIDI). It shows the name GP-5 and accepts one host at a time. Connect with a phone or a BLE-MIDI host on your computer. On a Mac, use Audio MIDI Setup › Bluetooth.
The radio starts while the logo shows. Calibration takes about one second and runs before the audio link. Starting the radio during an active link caused sound stops in testing.
MIDI messages reach fw_midi through the same callback as USB MIDI. The computer’s commands (SysEx) work over it too: macOS names the port “OpenGP5 Bluetooth” (“GP-5 Bluetooth” before 1.0); Launchpad and gp5_link.py (GP5_PORT="OpenGP5 Bluetooth") use it. Firmware updates need USB. Each pedal has its own address (from the chip’s efuse). The radio uses a short control-chip interrupt per event, 7.5 to 30 ms apart. It also uses 4 KB of RAM outside your firmware’s budget. The radio code is OpenGP5’s own (platform/nds32/bt/). DSP One header, dsp/firmware.h, compiled into the platform’s DSP program:
Callback When it runs static void fw_init(void) once, before audio starts static void fw_process(const int32_t *in, int32_t *out_left, int32_t *out_right) every block: 64 samples, mono in, stereo out, full scale ±2³¹. The platform applies the output level afterwards static void fw_param(uint32_t id, int32_t value) a parameter changed, before the next fw_process (a firmware with params.h defines it, even empty) static int fw_command(uint32_t cmd, const uint8_t *p, uint32_t n) the firmware’s own link commands from 0x7F11; return 0 for one it doesn’t know Use these tools in DSP code:
Tool Purpose gp5_param(id) Read the current parameter value gp5_reply, gp5_ack Reply to a command gp5_log Send a log line gp5_link_in(), gp5_link_out() Read or write audio-link words GP5_LARGE Put a buffer in the 122,880-byte area GP5_FAST Put time-critical code in the 19,712-byte area shared with variables GP5_CYCLES_LAST, GP5_CYCLES_WORST, GP5_LATE_BLOCKS Read audio timing counters GP5_CYCLE_COUNT() Time a piece of code in cycles The DSP budget is about 278,000 cycles per block at 44.1 kHz or 255,900 at 48 kHz. Code runs from flash unless you mark it for RAM. See Performance.
The audio link Set "audio": {"link": true} to exchange link_words 32-bit values each way per audio block. On the control chip, call gp5_link_start(on_block) in fw_init. The handler runs in an interrupt and must finish within one block.
On the DSP, read received words with gp5_link_in() and fill outgoing words with gp5_link_out(). A sample sent from the DSP returns from the control chip three blocks later: about 4.4 ms at 44.1 kHz or 4 ms at 48 kHz.
With link_early, the exchange starts at the beginning of the block. Define static void fw_link_early(const int32_t *in, int32_t *out) to supply new input before that exchange. See The audio link for the full example and timing rules.
USB audio A firmware written for platform 1.0 or later is a class-compliant USB audio interface unless firmware.json says "usb_audio": false. A firmware written for an older platform (or that doesn’t say) gets it only with "usb_audio": true. The pedal then shows up beside its USB-MIDI port (no driver on macOS, Windows or Linux): 2 channels each way, 16-bit, at the firmware’s sample rate.
Recording (pedal → computer) is the firmware’s finished stereo output, taken on the DSP after fw_process, before the computer’s playback is mixed in and before the volume knob. It reaches the computer sample for sample (the pedal sends 44 or 45 frames a millisecond, one more or fewer as its clock drifts from the computer’s). Playback (computer → pedal) is mixed into the outputs on the DSP, before the volume knob. The control processor resamples it from the computer’s clock to the DSP’s (they differ by tens of ppm). Direct sound. While the computer plays into the pedal, the pedal’s own sound can be left out of the outputs, so a DAW that monitors the pedal isn’t heard twice: gp5_usb_audio_set_direct(0) (1, the default, puts it back; gp5_usb_audio_direct() reads it). The computer can switch it too (Launchpad’s pedal panel, gp5_link.py direct off, 7E 19). Recording doesn’t change, and while nothing plays the pedal is always heard. It is back on after a restart, unless the firmware stores it and sets it again in fw_init. It travels in the audio link: the platform keeps 64 words each way after the firmware’s own link_words, and starts the link for a firmware that has none. So a firmware has at most 200 link words while USB audio is on. A firmware that finishes its sound on the control processor (NAM Loader) sets "usb_audio": {"record_from": "control"} and hands the output over from on_block: gp5_usb_audio_record(left, right), 64 samples each, full scale ±2^31 (a block it doesn’t hand over is recorded as silence, so the recording keeps its place). No words come back from the DSP for it then: link_words may be up to 264, but its own words towards the DSP must stay below 200 (the platform’s playback words are 200..263). Cost: on the control processor the USB interrupt (0.9 %) and the resampler in the link’s interrupt (about 3 % of a block, 6 % at worst); on the DSP a copy and a mix of 64 frames. "usb_audio": false gives all of it back. Log gp5_log("rate %ld, depth %d %%", rate, depth) on either processor. printf-style (%d %u %x %s %c %f, width, precision; gp5_fmt.h), at most about 110 characters a line, stamped with the time. The control chip keeps the last 4 KB; the DSP’s lines travel over the link and are marked dsp:. uint32_t is a long on both processors: print it with %lu / %lx. A DSP line costs a few thousand cycles: not every block.
python3 tools/gp5_link.py log -f # follow it while you play On the computer (tools/run_effect.py) the DSP’s gp5_log prints to the terminal.
Load and memory python3 tools/gp5_link.py status [--reset] The command shows current and peak block load, the longest main-loop pass, late blocks and memory use. Add --reset to clear peak readings. Test with the settings that use the most time before a release.
Trying things without a pedal python3 tools/simulate.py tremolo --script controls.txt --in guitar.wav The simulator runs both halves and the audio link with a control script. It saves screen images as PNGs and sound as a WAV file. To run the DSP half alone, use python3 tools/run_effect.py tremolo in.wav out.wav --set Rate=800 --set Shape=Square.
Talking to a running firmware Command Result or action gp5_link.py info the firmware’s name, version and author gp5_link.py params its parameters, values and ranges gp5_link.py set Rate 800 set one (a choice by name: set Shape Square) gp5_link.py presets, preset load / save / name <n> its presets gp5_link.py log [-f], status above Launchpad’s Live page uses these commands to read and edit settings. NAM Loader and Dreamcatcher have their own pages. See Protocols for the USB messages.
Versions These docs target platform 1.0.0. Its API was introduced in 0.7, so firmwares written for 0.7 or 0.8 build on 1.x unchanged; they get USB audio only if they ask for it ("usb_audio": true).
Read the running platform version from GP5_VERSION_TEXT in gp5_firmware.h. Set firmware.json’s platform field to the major and minor release your code needs, such as "1.0". The build rejects a newer minor version or a different major version.
1.x guarantees Every 1.x release preserves these parts:
Public calls, callbacks, their timing and manifest fields keep their meaning. Saved parameters, presets, store records and files remain readable. USB commands keep their numbers and existing fields. New reply fields go at the end. The platform stays within its memory share, leaving at least the documented firmware budgets. See Known limits for those budgets and Protocols for reply rules. Continuous integration (CI) runs build and test checks on changes. tools/check_budget.py checks memory use, and tools/test_compat.sh checks the fixtures in compat/1.0. The fixtures are the passthrough, the tremolo and the template as written for 1.0, and NAM Loader 1.3.1 as written for 0.8.
In 1.x, GP5_DEPRECATED warns that a call will go away. The warning must stay for at least one full minor release. A later major release can then remove the call. The guarantees do not cover code inside the platform or UI-kit struct layout beyond the fields you set. Limits such as link size and preset count may grow.

body:
This page covers USB commands, update steps, image files and the serial link between chips. Read How a firmware works to see where each part fits.
Source Role tools/gp5_flash.py USB message framing tools/gp5tool.py Update sessions tools/htfw.py Image format platform/nds32/proto.c, platform/nds32/dsp_link.c Control-processor commands platform/dsp/responder.c DSP commands Notation Byte sequences use hexadecimal (base 16). For fields longer than one byte, use little-endian order unless noted: send the least significant byte first. Angle brackets mark fields in a command. Square brackets mark parts you can leave out. In frame diagrams, brackets group the fields.
Mark Meaning u8, u16, u32, u64 Unsigned whole numbers of 8, 16, 32 or 64 bits i16 Signed 16-bit whole number f32 32-bit float NUL Zero byte ACK Reply that accepts a message NAK Reply that rejects a message or asks for a retry Nibble Four bits, or half a byte Commands marked 1.0 belong to the API that began in platform 0.7. These docs target platform 1.0.0. See Versions.
1. USB-MIDI framing The pedal uses USB-MIDI to send and receive frames. Each frame is one System Exclusive (SysEx) message:
F0 <body, every byte sent as two bytes: high nibble, then low nibble> F7 body = crc8, class, index, length, payload[length] crc8 = CRC-8, polynomial 0x07, initial value 0, not reflected, over the bytes 00, class, index, length, payload Class 0x01 sends a command with index 0. Class 0xFF sends update data. For data, the index is an 8-bit packet number that wraps back to 0. The pedal replies to update frames with 14 08 00. A non-zero third byte asks for the frame again.
2. Commands the open firmware answers (class 0x01) Update mode and DSP link Request payload Reply Action 11 6F 14 08 00 restart into the factory loader’s USB update mode (nothing is written) 7E 00 7E 00 <ok> <version u32> the DSP firmware’s version (platform DSP: 0x00010000) 7E 01 7E 01 <counters> <last frame> DSP link counters: frames, errors, ACKs, NAKs since start-up 7E 03 <off u16> <bytes…> 7E 03 <ok> stage up to 60 bytes of a DSP link payload at off 7E 04 <len u16> <wait> 7E 04 <status> <n> <reply…> send the staged payload to the DSP and wait up to wait × 10 ms; status 1 = reply frame, 0x14 = ACK, 0x13 = NAK, 0 = no answer Flash and stored data Request payload Reply Action 7E 05 <addr u32> <count> 7E 05 <ok> <bytes…> read up to 64 bytes of the control chip’s flash (below 2 MB, memory-mapped; reads only) 7E 06 7E 06 1 <JEDEC id u32> <status u32> the flash chip’s id and status register 1 7E 09 <addr u32> <count> 7E 09 <ok> <bytes…> the same as 7E 05, read with the flash controller’s read command (a driver check) 7E 07 <addr u32> 7E 07 <ok> erase a 4 KB sector of the storage area, 0x13F000–0x189FFF (reject other addresses; Storage) 7E 08 <addr u32> <bytes…> 7E 08 <ok> program up to 56 bytes (a multiple of 4) in the storage area 7E 0E <firmware id u32> 7E 0E <reloaded> the computer rewrote a store record (0.2.2+): the firmware’s fw_store_changed(id) (1.0: fw_storage_changed(); parameter records the platform reloads itself) loads it again (1) or can’t (0: restart the pedal) Controls, parameters and presets Request payload Reply Action 7E 10 <id u16> <value u32> 7E 10 <taken> set a value live (0.5.4). Parameter API: clamp a parameter to its range, send DSP-marked values, and save values with save flags (Parameters), ids past the parameters go to fw_param_set; 0 = not taken. Launchpad’s Live page 7E 11 <first u16> <count> 7E 11 <n> <values × n, 16 bits each> read values (0.5.4), at most 40; parameters are signed. n stops at the first id the firmware doesn’t know 7E 0F 7E 0F 1 <knob> <foot> <para> the controls (0.5.2+): volume knob 0..255 (filtered, as gp5_knob() gives it), foot switch and PARA push pressed now (0/1, not debounced). Launchpad turns its drawn knob with it 7E 12 <id u16> 7E 12 1 <count u16> <id u16> <flags> <unit> <min i16> <max i16> <default i16> <name> 0 <group> 0 <choices> 0 describe parameter id (1.0, Parameters); 7E 12 0 past the last one. Choices are A|B|C 7E 15 <id u16> <value i16> 7E 15 1 <text> 0 the text of a value (1.0, GP5_U_CUSTOM: the firmware’s fw_param_text); 7E 15 0 when it has none 7E 17 0 7E 17 1 <count> <current> <dirty> <used u64> presets (1.0): how many, the one loaded (FF = none), changed since (0/1), a bit per preset that holds a sound 7E 17 1 <n> / 7E 17 2 <n> 7E 17 <done> load / save preset n 7E 17 3 <n> 7E 17 1 <name> 0 preset n’s name 7E 17 4 <n> <name…> 7E 17 <done> rename preset n (printable ASCII, up to 12) Identity, load and log Request payload Reply Action 7E 0D 7E 0D 1 <major> <minor> <patch> <name…> 0 which firmware this is (platform 0.2.2 and later): the platform’s version and the firmware’s name (1.0: the manifest’s id; before: fw_name()) 7E 16 <offset u16> 7E 16 1 <total u16> <up to 48 bytes> the firmware’s metadata block from offset (1.0; 7E 16 0 for a firmware without a manifest). Format: "GP5META1", length u32, the manifest as JSON, NUL, padding to 4, CRC-32 of the JSON (platform/manifest.py) 7E 14 [1] 7E 14 1 <15 values, u32 each> load and memory (1.0). Control processor: cycles per block, audio-link handler last and worst, main loop’s longest pass (cycles), RAM used, RAM total. DSP: answered (0/1), cycles per block, last block, worst, late blocks, variables used and total, GP5_LARGE used and total. With 1: clear peak readings 7E 19 [on] 7E 19 1 <direct> <playing> <dry u32> <too much u32> <ppm i32> <waiting u16> <rec too much u32> <recording> USB audio (1.0): with on, 0 leaves the pedal’s own sound out of the outputs while the computer plays into the pedal (1 puts it back; USB audio). The reply: the setting, whether the computer is playing now, then counters since start-up: playback ran dry, playback frames dropped for want of room, the resampler’s clock correction (ppm), playback frames waiting, recording frames dropped, recording on. 7E 19 0 for a firmware without USB audio 7E 18 <from u32> 7E 18 1 <at u32> <end u32> <n> <n bytes> the log (1.0, gp5_log), from byte from. at = where the bytes start (the oldest kept, if from was overwritten), end = bytes written since start-up; ask again from at + n tools/gp5_link.py wraps 7E 00, 7E 01, 7E 03 / 7E 04, 7E 05 (flash-read) and the 1.0 commands (info, params, set, presets, preset, log, status). tools/gp5tool.py info reads 7E 16 too.
The state query 12 30 gets a reply from Valeton’s app or the factory loader:
State Reply Valeton app 11 30 01 00 Update mode 11 30 01 01 OpenGP5 app No reply to this query gp5tool.py status uses those replies and the USB port name (OpenGP5 from 1.0, GP-5 Open FW before, GP-5 for Valeton’s firmware and the loader) to tell the states apart.
Reply rules from 1.0: add new fields at the end. Keep old fields in place with the same meaning. Keep command numbers fixed. A reader must use the fields it knows and skip extra bytes. For new features, add a command or sub-command, such as 7E 17 5. Old tools can keep using the old commands. They need an update to use the new features.
3. Firmware update session (factory loader) Start update mode with 11 6F, or press and hold the foot switch and PARA while plugging the pedal in. Release both controls, then confirm update mode with gp5tool.py status or Launchpad. Use the reported state, not the screen alone. One update session writes one or more sections.
The platform restarts the chip before handing control to the loader. It writes a mark in the top 32 bytes of RAM at 0x20047FE0, outside the app’s RAM. On restart, the platform sees the mark before starting the link or firmware and enters the loader. This avoids a loader crash seen after direct handover from an active audio link. The extra restart takes about one second; the tools wait for it.
Send these frames in order. Wait for the loader to reply with 14 08 00 after each frame:
Step Bytes What happens ENTER 11 60 the session starts BEGIN 11 61 <type> 00 00 00 <packet count u32> <length u32> the loader erases that section DATA, once per packet class 0xFF, index = the packet number; 19 bytes each: 11 <type>, then the section’s data the data is written END 11 6E <type> 00 the section is done; BEGIN … END again for each further section (dsp, app, …) END_IMAGE 11 6E 6E 00 the pedal restarts length includes the two leading bytes 11 <type>. The loader can write the sections below, but not its own code at 0x0–0xFFFF. This preserves entry to update mode. A separate DSP updater fault can still block a flash; see J7 recovery.
Section Type Destination Maximum size dsp (DSP firmware) 0x63 DSP flash 0x4000 64 KB dsp-data (Valeton) 0x67 DSP flash 1 MB models (Valeton) 0x66 DSP flash 268 KB app (control processor) 0x62 flash 0x10000 1,440 KB presets (Valeton) 0x65 flash 0x190000 – 4. Image format (.bin) Valeton’s updates and this project’s builds use the same container. Little-endian:
0x00 'HTFW' 0x0C product name, 16 bytes ("GP-5") 0x08 u32 total file size 0x1C 'V' major minor patch (shown by Valeton's updater only) 0x21 u8 compression (0 = none) 0x22 u8 section count 0x24 u32 payload length 0x38 section table, 16 bytes per section: u16 CRC-16/MODBUS of the data, stored byte-swapped, u8 0, u8 type, u32 flash address, u32 offset of the data after the table, u32 length then the section data, in table order A Valeton image has all five sections. An OpenGP5 build has two: dsp and app. Use the order and addresses in the section table above. Run gp5tool.py check to check a file without a pedal.
5. Link between the processors (UART) The control chip’s UART0 (pins A0 receive / A1 transmit) and the DSP’s UART0 (0x40005000): 460800 baud, 8N1. Frames in both directions:
[crc8][length u16 = whole frame][01][payload] crc8 as in section 1, over the payload only payload = [cmd u16][len u16][fields…] status-only answer: 01 04 00 14 = ACK, 01 04 00 13 = NAK (bad CRC or length) Commands the platform uses:
Command Sender Payload / reply 0x6000 control version query, [cmd][8][0 u32] → [cmd][12][1 u32][version u32]. The control side waits for this answer before anything else. 0x1001 control output level: [cmd][12][sub 0 u32][f32 0.0 … 1.0] → ACK. The DSP is muted until it gets one. 0x4001 DSP a 24-byte status frame about every 43 ms (zeros today); not answered 0x7F01 / 0x7F02 control DSP flash tick patch: status / apply (see platform/dsp/tickpatch.h) 0x7F04 control DSP load: [cmd][8] or [cmd][12][1 u32] (clear peak readings) → [cmd][24][cycles last block][worst since start-up][late blocks][variables in use, bytes][GP5_LARGE in use, bytes] (1.0: the last two) 0x7F06 control USB audio (1.0): [cmd][12][off u32][0 u32] → ACK. 1 = leave the firmware’s sound out of the outputs (the computer’s playback stays); glides over a block 0x7F10 control a parameter (1.0): [cmd][12][id u32][value u32] → ACK; the DSP keeps it and calls fw_param() 0x4F10 DSP a log line (1.0, gp5_log): [cmd][len][text], not answered; the control chip adds it to its log as dsp: … 0x7F11 … 0x7FFF control the firmware’s own commands, handed to fw_command() (platform/dsp/gp5_dsp.h; from 0x7F10 for a firmware without parameters) Any other command is acknowledged.

These notes come from a GP-5 with main board GP-5_MB_V01_241115. Use platform/nds32/ for the control chip’s register code and platform/dsp/ for the sound chip’s code. Check your board against this one before using its pin map.
The DSP is the digital signal processor for sound. The control processor runs the screen, controls, USB and storage. It can also process sound. RAM holds working data; flash keeps code and saved data when power is off.
Control processor: MVsilicon BP1048B2 (Andes NDS32 V3, D1088 core) Clocks A phase-locked loop (PLL) multiplies the crystal clock to make the faster clocks used by the chip.
Clock or setting Value Crystal 24 MHz Main PLL and system clock 288 MHz by default; 320 MHz with "control": {"mhz": 320} Audio PLL 240 MHz; feeds USB through ÷4 and UART0 Core regulator at 320 MHz 1.25 V, matching Valeton’s firmware Regulator setup 0x40025040 bits 0–5 from efuse trim offset 0x14, then bit 21 Source platform/nds32/hal/clock.c The manifest has supported 320 MHz since platform 0.6.0. The efuse holds the chip’s factory trim values.
Flash and RAM The board has 2 MB of SPI flash, JEDEC ID 85 60 15, with no write-protected blocks. SPI is the serial bus used to reach the flash chip. JEDEC ID identifies that chip.
Range or address Contents 0x0–0xFFFF Factory loader; USB update tools cannot overwrite it 0x10000 App start, section 0x62; accepts up to 1,440 KB 0x13E168 End of Valeton’s V1.0.6 app 0x13F000–0x189FFF The installed build’s shared storage area 0x160000–0x161FFF Settings store, gp5_store_*, in two 4 KB sectors 0x170000 Valeton’s 100-byte preset-order table 0x171000–0x189FFF Working user-preset store when Valeton’s firmware runs 0x190000 Valeton factory presets, section 0x65 0x20000000–0x20047FFF RAM 0x20003000–0x20004000 App stack 0x20004000 Start of app data and bss; see platform/nds32/start/app.ld An app update erases the range it writes. The flash ranges above were checked with gp5_link.py flash-read. See Storage for the rules that keep file writes within the shared area.
App checks at start-up Before it starts the app, the factory loader checks these fields:
Field Expected value First 41 words Jumps (0x48……) into the image: reset, 8 exceptions and 32 interrupt lines Word at 0xC0 0xB0BEBDC9 Bytes 0xA4–0x105 The header layout in platform/nds32/start/vectors.S platform/nds32/pack.py checks the packed image against these rules.
Interrupts and pins An interrupt lets the chip handle an event before returning to the main code.
Line Source Task 0 Timer 1 1 ms tick 7 UART0 DSP link 8 Timer 2 LEDs UART is the serial link between the two chips. Pin names below match the chip’s port names. A low signal means ground level; a high signal means the pin’s logic-high level.
Pin Use A0 / A1 UART0 receive / transmit to the DSP A7 / A9 / A16 Screen data/command, chip select and reset; SPI master port 0 sends data A10 Screen backlight, timer 5 pulse-width modulation (PWM) A17 Foot switch; low when pressed A28 Volume knob, analog-to-digital converter (ADC) channel 9 A29 / A30 / A31 Blue / red / green for all three LEDs; high means on B2 / B3 PARA quadrature encoder; both high at a detent B6 PARA press; low when pressed A15, A22, A24, B5 Board outputs; board_init in main.c drives them as Valeton’s app does The screen is 160 × 80 colour pixels with an ST7735S-type SPI controller. USB uses full-speed device mode. The open firmware polls USB and shows the MIDI port and audio device name OpenGP5 (before 1.0: GP-5 Open FW).
DSP: Arm Cortex-M4F (marked JAT S95WT) Resource Value Clock About 191.9 MHz Audio Mono input, stereo output; 64 samples per block Default rate 44.1 kHz; 1.45 ms and about 278,000 cycles per block Optional rate 48 kHz; 1.33 ms and about 255,900 cycles per block 48 kHz setting "audio": {"sample_rate": 48000}, supported since 0.5.6 Audio clock register 0x4000e01c: 0x2029200f at 48 kHz, rather than 0x24f3200f at 44.1 kHz Measured 48 kHz block rate 749.8 blocks per second Flash 0x0–0x3FFF Valeton’s resident DSP boot and updater code Flash 0x4000 Section 0x63: 1 KB header, then OpenGP5 code Header word +0x0C Vector-table address, 0x4400 RAM 0x20000000–0x20007FFF (32 KB) and 0x10000000–0x1001FFFF (128 KB) Coprocessor 0x28000000 Programmable float unit; measured at 3 cycles per multiply-add The 48 kHz clock value is the second entry in Valeton’s DSP clock table. See platform/dsp/gp5_dsp.h for the memory your effect can use and the memory reserved for the platform. The extra float unit was no faster than the M4 in these tests, so the platform does not use it.
Debug header J7 J7 provides Serial Wire Debug (SWD). The triangle marks pin 1.
Pin Signal 1 Ground 2 Reset 3 SWCLK 4 SWDIO 5 SWO For the confirmed DSP update fault, follow J7 recovery.

body:
This page lists known faults, tested limits and features the platform does not provide. Report a problem if it does not appear here.
The hardware and flashing Reported DSP update fault As of November 2026, reports cover about seven GP-5s that ran or tried OpenGP5. Four reports describe a fault that stalls the DSP updater. This small sample cannot show how often the fault occurs across all GP-5s. These are reports of a fault in the pedal’s updater, not evidence that OpenGP5 caused it.
The fault blocks Valeton updates as well as OpenGP5. The flash stops at the start of a DSP section, before it writes that section. Tools may say stopped acknowledging at the erase; Valeton Suite may remain at 0 %. If the pedal still has its old build, unplugging and reconnecting it lets that firmware run.
The fix changes four bytes in the DSP updater. To get an OpenGP5 build onto an affected pedal, you need an FT232H USB debug adapter wired to J7 inside the case. Then gp5tool.py tickfix --apply can write the permanent fix. Read J7 recovery before starting. A pedal that a stalled flash leaves starting in update mode can run again without J7: Pedal stuck in update mode (gp5tool.py unstick, over USB).
Other flash and backup limits USB recovery has limits. The factory loader survives a USB update, but the DSP fault above can still block a flash. Use the OpenGP5 tools to go back. Valeton Suite can fail when returning from OpenGP5. Use Launchpad, the web flasher or gp5tool.py. Launchpad cannot back up Valeton SnapTones or user IRs. Export them in Valeton Suite before switching. Launchpad can save the 100 presets. Global settings stay on the pedal. The macOS MIDI service may not be ready. For an RtMidi -304 error before any data has been sent, the tools try up to three times. If a send has started, they stop and report the error instead of starting over. What firmware can use Both chips run C. The DSP, or digital signal processor, handles sound. The control chip runs the screen, controls, USB and storage. It can share sound work with the DSP.
Resource Limit Audio Mono input, stereo output; 44.1 or 48 kHz; 64-sample blocks DSP variables and fast code 19,712 bytes shared with GP5_FAST code DSP large buffers 122,880 bytes through GP5_LARGE DSP code and constants 38,920 bytes Control-processor RAM 264,160 bytes Control-processor code and constants About 1.4 MB Storage About 300 KB; store records up to 1 KB, files and up to 64 presets Parameters Signed whole numbers, −32,768 to 32,767; about 250 in one saved set Audio link Up to 264 32-bit words each way per block (200 while USB audio records from the DSP); round trip of three blocks Screen 160 × 80 pixels A round trip takes about 4.4 ms at 44.1 kHz or 4 ms at 48 kHz. A saved parameter set uses four bytes per entry in a 1 KB record. The 1.x memory promise holds for all of 1.x; tools/check_budget.py checks the budgets.
A different firmware starts with no saved data. Back up before you switch. The code does not use Valeton’s amp models or presets.
Features and processor limits USB audio is 16-bit, 2 in and 2 out, at the firmware’s sample rate. It costs about 4 % of the control processor and 64 words of the audio link each way. See USB audio. A build can use Bluetooth MIDI. Set "bluetooth": true in the manifest to turn on the radio. The radio code is OpenGP5’s own. Use USB to flash firmware. See Bluetooth. The control chip’s fused multiply-add instruction hangs the chip. The platform build does not use it. Its float unit needs about five cycles per operation. See Performance. Screen tools cover text and pixels. The UI kit adds settings pages and menus. The platform has no general line, shape or image drawing helpers. The build uses C with no standard C library. It has its own code for maths and text. The tools The web flasher uses Web MIDI. Use Chrome, Edge or Opera on a computer. Safari lacks this feature; Firefox asks for permission. The page downloads OpenGP5 builds. For other catalog builds, download the image and drop it on the page so it can check the file. Your system may warn you when you open Launchpad. The app has no code signature. Use the install steps to open it. The simulator runs scripts and saves screen images; it has no live window. It does not measure processor speed. Check timing on the pedal. NAM Loader runs the A2-Lite part of A2 captures. It does not support older A1 captures.
