body:
Some GP-5s have a DSP updater fault that blocks firmware updates, including Valeton’s updates. The flasher may report “stopped acknowledging at the erase of the dsp section”, or Valeton Suite may remain at 0 %. This guide uses a USB debug adapter to get past the fault, install OpenGP5, and write a permanent fix. The DSP is the digital signal processor that handles sound.
Symptoms (all of them):
The flash stops at the start of a DSP part (dsp, dsp-data or models), before anything is written to it. It happens every time, with every tool: Launchpad, the web flasher, gp5tool.py, Valeton Suite. The app part (app) and the presets (presets) on their own do flash. If the pedal starts after you unplug and reconnect it, its old build still runs. Use this guide to get past the fault when installing a new build. If the pedal now always starts in update mode (the BOOTLOAD screen), first get it working again over USB: see Pedal stuck in update mode.
Cause. After the DSP updater resets its flash memory, a brief read fault can send its timer to the wrong address. The updater then waits for a counter that does not change. The fix changes four bytes so the counter uses an address that avoids the fault. You need to run OpenGP5 on the pedal to apply it. Want to help find a way to apply it without opening the pedal? See DSP updater fault: help wanted.
Risk. This procedure means opening the pedal, wiring J7 and using a debugger. Wiring errors can damage the pedal. Step 2 reads memory. Step 3 changes RAM for one powered session. Step 4 flashes firmware, and step 6 writes a permanent change to the DSP updater. The tools check for the known updater before applying its fix. Stop if those checks fail.
Pedal stuck in update mode An update that stalls never finishes, so the pedal’s loader keeps starting in update mode. gp5tool.py unstick gets it out over USB, without J7 and without the DSP. You need Valeton’s GP-5 firmware file (V1.0.6, from Valeton’s site; the full update with all five sections).
python3 tools/gp5tool.py unstick GP-5_USB_V1.0.6_20250626.bin Then unplug the pedal and plug it in again without holding any buttons. It starts Valeton’s firmware.
It installs Valeton’s app and presets, and writes the loader’s “update complete” marker as part of the presets. It erases the pedal’s global settings and any IRs saved in Valeton’s firmware, which share that part of flash. If an OpenGP5 firmware’s DSP part did get onto the pedal before, add --app <that firmware's .bin> so the app matches it. It doesn’t touch the DSP. Updates still stall afterwards: the rest of this page fixes that. What you need An FT232H USB board (the common “CJMCU-232H” or Adafruit FT232H breakout). An ESP-Prog (FT2232H) also works with --adapter esp-prog. A 470 Ω resistor (anything from about 200 to 500 Ω). Three short wires. Soldering them to J7 is the most reliable; small test clips or header pins pressed into the holes can work. A computer with Python 3.9 or later and OpenGP5’s tools (the tools folder from the OpenGP5 download: pip install mido python-rtmidi). An OpenGP5 firmware image (.bin) with tickfix support, such as the current tremolo, Dreamcatcher or NAM Loader build. These docs target platform 1.0.0. OpenOCD, the debugger program: macOS: brew install open-ocd Linux: sudo apt install openocd (or your distribution’s package) Windows: OpenOCD from the xPack project (xpack-openocd), and once, the WinUSB driver for the FT232H with Zadig (pick the FT232H’s “Interface 0”, WinUSB, “Replace driver”). Wiring J7 is a row of five holes on the main board, next to the chip marked JAT (the DSP). Pin 1 is marked with a triangle.
J7 pin Signal FT232H 1 (triangle) GND GND 2 RST not connected 3 SWCLK AD0 4 SWDIO AD1 through the 470 Ω resistor, and AD2 directly 5 SWO not connected Put the resistor between AD1 and pin 4, and run AD2 straight to pin 4. AD1 sends data and AD2 reads it; the resistor keeps the two from fighting when the pedal answers. Some FT232H boards label the pins D0, D1, D2 instead of AD0, AD1, AD2. On an ESP-Prog the same pins are TCK (AD0), TDI (AD1) and TDO (AD2).
Plug the pedal and the FT232H into the same computer so they share a ground. The pedal can be powered from its USB cable as usual.
Steps Run these in the OpenGP5 folder (where tools is).
1. Enter update mode and check the status. Unplug the pedal. Press and hold the foot switch and PARA. Plug it back in, then release both controls. Confirm the mode with the tool below; do not rely on the screen alone. A pedal on the BOOTLOAD screen may already be in update mode.
python3 tools/gp5tool.py status Expected result: update mode.
2. Check for the known stall. This step reads memory without changing it.
python3 tools/j7_nudge.py check Expected result: The DSP's updater is stalled the known way. For a connection error, see Troubleshooting.
3. Apply the temporary RAM change. This gets the updater past the stall for this powered session. Unplugging clears the change:
python3 tools/j7_nudge.py nudge Expected result: Done: the updater's timer counts again.
4. Flash the full OpenGP5 image. Keep the pedal powered after step 3:
python3 tools/gp5tool.py flash GP-5_tremolo.bin --sections all Use the path to your chosen image in place of GP-5_tremolo.bin. It must support tickfix. Expected result: the flash completes, including its DSP section.
5. Start the installed build. Unplug and reconnect the pedal without holding the controls. Expected result: the new OpenGP5 build starts.
6. Check and apply the permanent fix. The first command reads its state. The second writes four bytes to the DSP updater in two small writes, without an erase:
python3 tools/gp5tool.py tickfix python3 tools/gp5tool.py tickfix --apply Expected results: not applied, then applied: updates won't stall. If the first command says the fix is already applied, you do not need to apply it again.
Finish. Unplug the pedal and adapter before removing the wires. The permanent fix lets this updater complete the USB flash steps that the fault blocked. Run gp5tool.py tickfix to check the fix’s state. Other flash faults still need their own checks.
Troubleshooting OpenOCD can’t connect (“Error connecting DP”, no DAP info): check the three wires first. If they’re right, unplug both devices before checking the SWCLK and SWDIO connections against the pin table. On Linux, OpenOCD may need permission for USB devices (run it once with sudo, or add a udev rule for 0403:6014). On Windows, the FT232H needs the WinUSB driver (Zadig). check says the debug port answered but the DSP didn’t power up its debug side: the wiring works (the port’s ID was read), but the debug side didn’t start, most likely because the DSP itself isn’t running. Unplug the pedal, plug it in again, and run check within a second or two. If it still fails, report it with what check printed: this is not solved yet. check says it isn’t the known stall: pc ... isn't in the updater's wait: the pedal isn’t in update mode, or it isn’t stalled (it may be a pedal that doesn’t have this problem). Do step 1 again. the vector table was already moved: you already ran nudge in this session: go on with step 4. the DSP's vector table isn't the one this was made for: your pedal’s updater is a different version from the one this fix was made on. Stop here and report it (below): nothing was changed. tickfix --apply says the updater “isn’t the known one”: the same: report it, nothing was written. The flash in step 4 still stops: unplug the pedal, start again at step 1, and report it with the output. Reporting results Whether it worked or not, please open a hardware report with the output from j7_nudge.py check and gp5tool.py tickfix. Include the pedal and tool versions. Reports help track which pedals have the fault and which updater versions the fix supports.

body:
Some GP-5s cannot update their DSP: every flash stops at the start of a DSP section, with every tool, Valeton Suite included. The cause is known and a four-byte fix exists, but on a pedal that stalls, installing that fix needs the pedal opened and a debug adapter wired to J7 (J7 recovery). This page is for contributors who want to help find a way to apply the fix over USB, without opening the pedal.
Status, November 2026: about seven GP-5s have reported in; four have the fault. The fix is tested on one of them.
What goes wrong The DSP’s flash starts with Valeton’s resident updater (DSP flash 0x0–0x3FFF). The pedal’s loader resets the DSP into it at the start of every update. Its flash set-up resets the flash chip and then waits 12 SysTick ticks.
On affected pedals, memory-mapped flash reads in that window come back with bit 7 of byte 0 of each 32-bit word cleared. The SysTick handler runs from flash and loads the tick counter’s address from a literal at DSP flash 0xB60: 0x20000DC0 reads as 0x20000D40. The handler counts in the wrong word; the wait, which runs from a RAM copy (its literal is at flash 0x16DC), reads the right one. The wait never ends, and the update stalls before the first erase. (The wrong word happens to be the command word of the flash-reset descriptor, so a stalled updater also slowly corrupts that.)
What clears the fault, and why only some pedals have it, is not known.
The resident updater is not in Valeton’s update file. The file’s DSP sections start at DSP flash 0x4000. The resident can only be read from a pedal over J7. Nothing from it is published here.
The fix Both literals are changed from 0x20000DC0 to 0x20000000, whose byte 0 has no bit 7, so a faulty read gives the same value as a good one. 0x20000000 holds dead code in the resident’s RAM image, and the wait compares an unsigned difference, so the counter’s starting value doesn’t matter. The change only clears bits: two 2-byte page programs, no erase, safe to repeat after an interruption. SysTick runs only in the update path, so normal start-up never uses these words.
platform/dsp/tickpatch.h applies it from OpenGP5’s DSP firmware. Its header explains how: it copies the resident’s RAM image where the resident puts it, then calls the resident’s own page-program routine from a small RAM stub, with interrupts off. It refuses any resident whose hash isn’t the known one. gp5tool.py tickfix reports the state; --apply applies it. tools/dsp_tickfix_emu.py checks the patcher and the stall in an emulator (Unicorn), without a pedal. It needs a resident read from a pedal. The catch: the patcher runs inside OpenGP5’s DSP firmware, and getting that firmware onto the DSP is the flash that stalls. Today, J7 breaks that loop by moving the counter by hand once (j7_nudge.py).
What is known not to work A fix inside the dsp section. The loader resets the DSP into the resident for every update session, so nothing in the dsp section runs at that point. The resident fixing itself. Its updater accepts a write to its own area, but it stalls before it takes any command. Valeton Suite. It uses the same updater and stalls the same way. The control processor writing DSP flash. It flashes its own app without the stall, but no path from it to the DSP’s flash is known. The open problem Find a way to clear those four bytes on a pedal that stalls, using only USB. What still works on such a pedal:
The control processor’s app (app) and the presets flash normally, so an OpenGP5 app can be installed. Valeton’s DSP firmware keeps running, and the app can pass commands to it: Valeton’s DSP firmware: link commands lists what is known. If an update left the pedal starting in update mode, gp5tool.py unstick gets it running again (Pedal stuck in update mode). Leads 1. SnapTone uploads. Valeton Suite uploads SnapTones to a running pedal, with no update session. User IRs are no help here: they are stored in the control processor’s flash (0x1BE000 on), not the DSP’s.
Where does a SnapTone upload land: DSP flash, DSP RAM, or the control processor’s flash? If DSP flash: Valeton’s DSP firmware has its own flash-write path. Is the target address checked? Could a crafted upload clear two bytes at 0xB60 and 0x16DC? The slot-management commands (0x7001, 0x7003, and 0x2001, 0x2003 for cabinets) are listed with their handler addresses but not decoded. 2. The other DSP commands. Is there one that writes memory, or one whose length checks let it run code? A small stub would be enough: the resident’s own page-program routine does the writing, as tickpatch.h shows.
3. A wiring check. J7 carries the DSP’s SWD lines. If SWDIO and SWCLK also reach pins of the control processor (BP1048), OpenGP5 could do the J7 step itself from the app. Needed: a continuity check between each J7 pin and the BP1048’s pins on an opened pedal, with the pedal unplugged. The pinout is in J7 recovery.
4. The flash chip itself. The DSP’s flash is a separate SPI NOR chip. A clip-on programmer could clear the four bytes with the DSP held in reset. This still means opening the pedal, but no debug wiring. Untested; the chip’s position and type aren’t documented yet.
What else would help Reports from more pedals, with or without the fault, so we learn how common it is. The resident’s fingerprint from affected pedals. The fix refuses any resident but the known one. If the four affected pedals have different residents, each needs checking. j7_nudge.py check compares the resident’s vector table with the known one over J7, read-only. Caveats The read-fault model comes from one pedal. If other pedals lose other bits, the patch may not be enough. Two UART interrupt vectors and one more literal in the resident also have bit 7 set in byte 0; the patch can’t fix them by clearing bits. They matter only if the control processor sends data during the ~12-tick window after the flash reset. It doesn’t seem to, but that isn’t measured. After the fix, a J7 nudge must target 0x20000000; j7_nudge.py refuses a patched resident. Ground rules No Valeton code or data in the repository: no disassembly listings, dumps or copied bytes. Work from your own copy of Valeton’s firmware file (V1.0.6 from Valeton’s site) and describe findings in your own words, with addresses. Nothing that writes the resident (0x0–0x3FFF) goes on a pedal except the four-byte bit-clear above. A broken resident takes away the DSP’s update path. Read-only experiments first. Anything that writes needs a tested way back. Share findings in an issue or pull request. Contributors are credited by their GitHub handle.

What Valeton’s DSP firmware (V1.0.6, the dsp section) understands on the link from the control processor. It was worked out from both firmwares and checked on a pedal. It is here for the DSP updater fault work: on a pedal whose updates stall, Valeton’s DSP firmware stays installed, and an OpenGP5 app can talk to it.
Addresses are DSP addresses in Valeton’s V1.0.6 (its dsp section is loaded at DSP flash 0x4000) or, marked “control”, addresses in Valeton’s control-processor app (runtime address = file offset + 0x10000). Other versions differ. Everything here comes from reading the code and from tests on one pedal; treat it as notes, not a spec.
Sending a command from a computer The link itself (UART, 460800 baud, framing, CRC) is in Protocols, section 5. OpenGP5’s control firmware passes any payload through to the DSP and returns the answer: 7E 03 stages the payload, 7E 04 sends it (Protocols). From Python:
import gp5_link as gl # tools/gp5_link.py link = gl.open_link() print(gl.raw(link, bytes.fromhex("00600800 00000000"))) # 0x6000: version query link.close() raw() returns (status, reply): status 1 with the reply payload, 0x14 for ACK, 0x13 for NAK, or None.
Not tested yet: today’s OpenGP5 platform running with Valeton’s DSP firmware. An early control firmware of this project did exactly this (November 2026) and drove Valeton’s DSP to full sound with the commands below. The platform’s start-up only needs the version answer, which Valeton’s DSP gives.
Payloads and dispatch Payload = [cmd u16][len u16 = payload length][fields], little-endian. The command’s high nibble is the group, the low 12 bits the index. Valeton’s dispatcher (0x5C68, jump table at 0x5CD2) has one handler table per group:
group table handlers 0 0x8DD0 7 1 0x8E04 2 2 0x8E0C 4 3 0x8E34 1 (empty) 4 0x8E38 3 5 0x8E44 3 6 0x8E5C 5 7 0x8E1C 6 Answers: a status-only frame 01 04 00 14 (ACK) for “set” commands, a data frame for queries, nothing for a few. A bad CRC or length gets 01 04 00 13 (NAK).
Commands cmd payload after [cmd][len] DSP handler control sender notes 0x0000 whole preset, len 0x170 (below) 0x5314 0x465F0 load, state = 3 0x0001 u8 module, u8 param, u16 –, u32 model index, f32 value (len 0x10) 0x5346 0x46B94 one parameter; ignored if module ≥ 10 0x0002 u32 which, u32 value (len 0xC): 0 = preset volume, 1 = BPM 0x53A0 0x46678, 0x466A8 0x0003 u8 order[10] (len 0x10) 0x53CC 0x466D8 only a permutation of 0..9 is applied 0x0004 u8 module, u8 on (len 8) 0x537E 0x46AFC module on/off 0x0005 u8 module, u8 flag, u16 model, 8 × f32 (len 0x28) 0x5330 0x46B3C module model 0x0006 u32 arg 0x52F6 0x46AC4 0x1000 global settings, len 0x10 (below) 0x5084 0x4658C 0x1001 u32 sub, 4-byte value (len 0xC) 0x50C8 0x468EC one field of 0x1000; sub 0 = output level (f32) 0x2001 not decoded: cabinet / user IR slot management 0x50F4 0x16678 upload path, see the fault page 0x2002 u32 id → 76-byte module info 0x51D0 0x163DC cabinet list, ids 0–39 0x2003 not decoded: cabinet / user IR slot management 0x519C 0x165F4 upload path 0x4000 u8, u8, u16 0x56B0 0x46C08 looks like the tuner (reference pitch) 0x4001 DSP → control, 20-byte report about every 43 ms 0x5720 (on request) 0x4002 u16 –, u16 value 0x56EC 0x46C60 0x5000 u16 which (0–2), u16 value 0x5022 0x4680C … 0x5001 u8, u8, u8 0x500E 0x46844 0x5002 u32 0 → data 0x4FFA 0x46770 crashes the DSP unless 0x5000/0x5001 came first 0x6000 u32 0 → 12-byte version 0x5652 0x46714 0x6001 u32 flag 0x5604 0x46740 0x6002 u32 0, u32 0 → two floats 0x567C 0x46884 0x6003 u32 state: 0 = output held, 3 = run 0x5630 0x46A34 0x6004 u32 flag 0x55D8 0x468BC 0x7001 not decoded: SnapTone (Tone Catch) slot management 0x55A8 0x16B30 upload path 0x7002 u32 id → 76-byte module info 0x551E 0x16864 SnapTone list, ids 0–79 0x7003 not decoded: SnapTone slot management 0x54EC 0x16AAC upload path 0x7004 empty the control side has a handler for a 0x7004 frame (0x42FDC) 0x7005 u32 → 16-byte echo, then ACK 0x54AE 0x16890 “state” and “action” are two bytes of the DSP’s control block at 0x20002098 + 0x2E0 / +0x2E1.
Module info (76 bytes): [u16 id][u16][u32][16-byte name][16-byte name][8 × f32 parameters].
0x0000 whole preset (0x170 bytes) offset field +0x04 f32 preset volume +0x08 u16 BPM +0x0A u16 module enable mask (bit n = module n) +0x0C u8 order[10] +0x18 u8 model index[10]: position in that module’s list +0x24 u8 flag[10]: byte 9 of the model’s catalog record +0x30 10 × 8 × f32 parameters The ten modules: 0 noise gate, 1 boost/comp, 2 drive, 3 amp, 4 cabinet, 5 EQ, 6 modulation, 7 delay, 8 reverb, 9 SnapTone. A wrong flag crashes the DSP when it applies the preset (it calls a missing callback).
0x1000 global settings (0x10 bytes) +0x04 f32 (sub 4), +0x08 f32 output level (sub 0), +0x0C s8 (sub 1), +0x0D u8 (sub 2), +0x0E u8 (sub 3), +0x0F s8 (sub 5). Only the output level’s meaning is known.
Start-up and sound Valeton’s control app, after the version query, lists the modules (0x2002 for ids 0–39, 0x7002 for 0–79, then 0x7005) and sends: 0x1000, 0x1001 sub 0 = 0 (mute), 0x6003 0, 0x0000, 0x6003 0. The DSP is silent until 0x6003 3 (run) and 0x1001 sub 0 = 1.0 (output level) follow.
When the DSP crashes A crash (wrong preset flag, 0x5002 sent first) stops all answers; the pedal goes silent. Unplug the pedal and plug it in again: the DSP starts Valeton’s firmware afresh. Nothing in flash changes, as long as the commands sent didn’t write it.
Open Groups 2 and 7: the slot-management commands (0x2001, 0x2003, 0x7001, 0x7003). Where do their writes go? The meaning of “state” / “action” in the DSP’s main loop; groups 4 and 5 beyond the notes above.

Using it Can I go back to Valeton’s firmware? Yes. Follow Recovery to flash the full update. The pedal starts with factory presets. Restore a Launchpad backup to get your own presets back. Before leaving Valeton’s firmware, export SnapTones and user IRs in Valeton Suite; Launchpad cannot back them up.
Can a flash leave the pedal unable to start? A failed flash can stop the installed app from starting. The factory loader remains available for USB recovery. Some pedals also have a DSP update fault that blocks a new flash, including Valeton’s updates. Those pedals may need a debug adapter wired inside the case. If a stalled flash leaves the pedal starting in update mode, gp5tool.py unstick gets it running again over USB, without opening it: see Pedal stuck in update mode. Read Known limits and J7 recovery before you flash.
Does OpenGP5 use Valeton’s models or presets? No. The firmware contains no code or data from Valeton or the chip vendor.
Does Bluetooth work? You can choose to add Bluetooth MIDI to a build. It sends MIDI messages to the effect over the radio. It does not send audio. Use USB to flash firmware. See Bluetooth.
Can the pedal be an audio interface? Yes. A firmware built for 1.0 is a USB audio interface with 2 inputs and 2 outputs, unless it turns it off. The computer records the firmware’s finished sound and can play through the pedal. See USB audio.
Does my data survive a change of firmware? A different firmware ID starts with empty storage. Back up before switching. Launchpad offers a backup if it can read the installed build. An update with the same ID keeps storage; check its release notes for changes to saved settings.
Which effects can I try? OpenGP5 provides NAM Loader, Dreamcatcher and the tremolo. See the firmware guides for controls and downloads. Other authors can list builds in the catalog. Those builds carry Not reviewed: file checks do not include a source-code review.
Writing firmware Do I need a pedal to start? No. The simulator runs the code and saves sound and screen files. The template can build in GitHub Codespaces, in your browser. You need a pedal to check timing and hardware behavior.
Which platform version should I use? 1.0, the version these docs target. Firmwares written for 0.7 or 0.8 build on it unchanged. See Versions.
What language can I use? The build uses C99 on both chips, with no standard C library. The platform supplies maths (gp5_math.h) and printf-style text formatting (gp5_fmt.h).
Where should I put the sound code? Start on the DSP, the digital signal processor. If it runs out of time or memory, move work to the control chip through the audio link. Use Performance to measure each side.
How much sound processing fits? NAM Loader runs an amp model and a 1,024-tap cab IR. Dreamcatcher runs a looper, grain delay and reverb. Both split work across the chips. A small tremolo on the DSP uses a few percent of its time budget.
Can I use C++ or a C library? The platform build supports C. Code that needs only integer types and maths may need few changes to run here. Code that depends on malloc, host files or threads needs more work; the platform does not provide those calls.
Can I include code from Valeton or the chip vendor’s SDK? No. OpenGP5 and its catalog exclude code, headers, libraries, firmware and data from those sources.
How do I save settings? Declare parameters and mark which ones to save or include in presets. The platform handles saving and lets Launchpad edit them. For other data, use Storage.
Does the pedal have stereo input? No. The guitar input is mono. The outputs are stereo.
Can I use 48 kHz? Yes. Set "audio": { "sample_rate": 48000 } in firmware.json. Each 64-sample block then lasts 1.33 ms.
How do I share my build? Follow Releasing your firmware.
The project Who makes OpenGP5? A few people work on it in their spare time under the OpenGP5 name. The project has no affiliation with Valeton.
How can I help? Send a hardware report with successes and faults. You can also write an effect or improve the docs. See Contributing.

Get started Flash from your browser USB9V VOLPARA IN OUT/PHONES USB9V VOLPARA IN OUT/PHONES USB9V VOLPARA IN OUT/PHONES NAM LoaderDreamcatcherTremolo Play Play NAM amp models. Add the sound of a speaker cab with a cabinet impulse response (cab IR). Or loop your guitar with Dreamcatcher's delay and reverb.
Choose firmware Manage Use Launchpad to flash firmware, load sounds, edit presets and back up supported data. It runs on macOS, Windows and Linux.

static void fw_process(const int32_t *in, int32_t *out_left, int32_t *out_right) { for (uint32_t i = 0; i < GP5_BLOCK; i++) { float wave = 0.5f + 0.5f * sinf(2.0f * GP5_PI * phase); float gain = 1.0f - depth * wave; phase += step; if (phase >= 1.0f) phase -= 1.0f; out_left[i] = out_right[i] = (int32_t)((float)in[i] * gain); } } Before you flash: a known DSP update fault can block a USB flash and may need a debug adapter wired inside the pedal.
